items.body: A Vilnius-based Indonesian composer and a Berlin-based Japanese producer have recorded an album in three different nations and released it on an Ugandan imprint. As a result, Abu sounds as if it comes from nowhere and everywhere at once: a “mystifying new landmass, an imaginary island of ash.” To honor the spirit of the release, today’s review was born on one continent and the interview on another. Along the way, one will hear shavings of sound from each artist’s home. Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi and Shigeru Ishihara intermingle gamelan percussion and taiko rhythms with chants and shouts that seem to come from deepest Africa or from the heart of the volcano. The music imitates lava: erupting, flowing, burning and solidifying. Once it has disrupted the elements around it, Abu incorporates them into a new sonic landmass. In “Hai no uta,” two rings of an Indonesian bell preface more abrasive grinds and growls. A Javanese gong is struck; a high flute wails; a miniaturized choir sings a tiny song, recalling the Shobijin. The tension rises as the percussion begs to break through; and on “Abu,” it does. The tribal rhythms and guttural utterances recall KINACT’s Kinshasa in Action, also on Nyege Nyege Tapes; the continents seem connected again, honoring Pangea. The deep bass of “Palau” reflects subterranean rumble: while over too soon, it gives way to the even more enthralling “Wujud,” whose industrial stumbles and starts are melded to mechanical glissandos, an Orcan, deep earth factory. “Hino Tori” is a wild outlier, bursting forth with bangha rhtymns reminiscent of “Get Your Freak On” and swiftly adding a pounding techno beat; one can imagine this as a club killer on any continent. The metallic middle teases a far different audience before finishing a water bottle and plunging back in, even more energized than before. Those waiting for their thrash moment will find it on the chaotic, ensuing piece: a far cry from the Indonesian bells that launched the set only half an hour before. The LP’s primary draw, outside of its stunning juxtapositions of timbre, is its reaffirmation of a world without borders. Over countless millennia, magma has created innumerable landmasses, while the sea has often impassively reclaimed its own. Human borders mean nothing to geologic time. Abu is a reminder of the wealth of international music: entire species of music that much of the general public has yet to discover. We need not fear such encounters, as they do not threaten our own identity; quite the contrary. Instead, as in the case of Takkak Takkak, they broaden our language and deepen our experience. (Richard Allen) Takkak Takkak photo by @mr_guep Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi has kindly taken time out of Takkak Takkak’s touring schedule to answer a few questions about the production process for Abu. Your self-titled debut introduced a thrilling collision between DIY instrument building, Javanese traditions, Japanese electronics, noise, gabber and ritual percussion, often with a raw, playful sense of excess. On Abu, those same elements seem to have become part of a much broader imaginary world—less confrontational perhaps, but more immersive and narrative. Did you consciously set out to expand the language you established on the first album, and what did this fictional “island of ash” allow you to express that the debut could not? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: I don’t think we approached Abu by asking how to expand what we had done on the first album. It was more about continuing a conversation that had already started. By the time we began working on Abu, we had spent more time playing together, building trust and understanding how each other’s ideas and sounds could interact. Naturally, the music started to move into different directions. With the first album, we were discovering the chemistry between us. There was a lot of direct energy finding out what happens when handmade instruments, distorted electronics, ritual rhythms and dance music collide. Everything felt immediate and physical. For Abu, we had already developed a shared language, so we didn’t need to prove that those elements could coexist. Instead, we could ask where they might take us. The fictional island became a useful way of thinking because it isn’t Indonesia, Japan or anywhere else. It is a place where histories, myths, disasters and dreams can exist together without having to explain themselves. Ash is also an interesting material. It can represent destruction, but it is also what remains after transformation. New life often grows from volcanic ash. So Abu became less about representing a culture and more about imagining how things constantly disappear, mutate and re-emerge. One of the most fascinating aspects of Abu is the way it dissolves fixed notions of place and identity. The album was recorded across Yogyakarta, Švenčionėliai and Berlin, while drawing on Indonesian, Japanese and Baltic sonic environments without allowing any of them to dominate. Rather than presenting cultural traditions as fixed inheritances, the record seems to imagine them as constantly shifting landscapes. How did the experience of working across these different locations reshape your understanding of home, identity and collaboration? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: For me, identity has never been something fixed. Even traditional music is always changing. Every generation changes instruments, techniques and contexts. Tradition survives because people keep transforming it. Recording in Yogyakarta, Lithuania and Berlin reinforced that feeling. Each place has its own atmosphere, but we weren’t trying to collect local sounds like souvenirs. We were more interested in how our listening changed when we moved through different environments. Sometimes collaboration is less about combining different cultures than about creating a third space where nobody completely owns the result anymore. That’s what interests me. Instead of saying, “This is Indonesian,” or “This is Japanese,” we try to build a shared sonic ecology where those categories become less important than the relationships between sounds. In that sense, home is not only a geographical place. Home can also be a process of making things together. Your debut album was stylistically cohesive even with incursions into techno on tracks like “Salamander” and was driven by rhythm. One of the most striking aspects of Abu is its constant transformation and reflective nature. Ritual percussion gives way to hard dance rhythms, handmade instruments dissolve into electronic textures, and tracks such as “Api” and “Hino-Tori” move effortlessly between ceremony, ecstatic propulsion and the dance floor, while quieter moments like “Pulau”, “Nimbal” or “Funka suru mizu” provide spaces of suspension. Yet none of these shifts feels abrupt or arbitrary. How do you approach composition when working together? Do these transformations emerge intuitively through improvisation and experimentation, or is there an underlying architecture that allows such radically different musical languages to coexist so naturally? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: Our process is actually very fluid. We improvise a lot because that’s how we discover unexpected relationships between sounds. But improvisation is only the beginning. Afterwards we spend a lot of time listening, editing and thinking about how one sound transforms into another. We’re less interested in contrasting genres than in following the energy inside the sound itself. A ritual drum pattern and a gabber kick might seem completely different stylistically, but physically they both work on the body. They both produce collective movement, trance or repetition. Once you stop thinking in terms of genre and start thinking in terms of vibration, rhythm and texture, those transitions become quite natural. The quieter pieces are equally important because they allow the listener to breathe. Silence, space and suspension are also forms of rhythm. Without those moments, the more intense passages wouldn’t have the same impact. So there is structure, but it usually emerges after experimentation rather than before it. Both of your other projects—Raja Kirik (Johanes “Mo’ong” Santoso Pribadi with Yennu Ariendra) and Scotch Rolex (Shigeru Ishihara)—have always challenged musical categories, but Takkak Takkak seems driven as much by joy, humour and curiosity as by experimentation itself. In a musical landscape that often takes experimental music very seriously, especially within an ethnological framework, does playfulness become a creative strategy for opening listeners up to unfamiliar sounds and ways of listening? Johanes “Mo’ong” Santos Pribadi: I think play is a very serious activity. When people hear the word “experimental,” they sometimes expect something difficult or intellectual. But curiosity usually begins with play. Children don’t separate learning from playing; they explore because they’re curious. I think music can work in the same way. Humour also helps remove fear. If listeners feel that they have to understand everything intellectually, they might close themselves off. But if they can laugh, dance or simply become curious, they’re already listening differently. In projects like Raja Kirik and Takkak Takkak, we’re interested in transformation rather than preservation. Traditional culture has always contained humour, absurdity, masks, tricksters and moments of chaos. Those aspects are just as important as the ceremonial or sacred ones. So playfulness isn’t there to make the work lighter. It’s another way of opening possibilities. Once people stop worrying about categories traditional versus contemporary, ritual versus club music, acoustic versus electronic they become more willing to experience sound on its own terms. (Interview by Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — (This review originally appeared on my website progblog.co.uk on 21st December 2021)Locanda delle Fate's Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi� (Polydor, 1977) is quite rightly regarded as one of the best progressivo italiano albums of the 70s but it is also a classic example of the right record at the wrong time, as it was released when symphonic prog and long suites in general had begun to be ignored by a new generation of music fans. They disbanded in 1980.The resurgent interest in progressive rock in the 1990s, reappraising the music of a generation before, was sufficiently broad to include Locanda delle Fate, and their debut album was released on CD, with bonus tracks in 1990. The group reformed in 1996 and released the more straightforward rock CD Homo Homini Lupus three years later, then regrouped in 2010 and played their farewell tour in 2017.One of the main songwriters was Michele Conta (fifth from the left in the Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi� inner gatefold group photo) who joined the band as a pianist just aged 17. Conta was largely responsible for the romantic influences, hinting at the keyboard work of Tony Banks but perhaps more accurately, creating a sound that fitted the vocals of Leonardo Sasso and generating comparisons with the music of Banco del Mutuo Soccorso. Conta was born in the Piemonte city of Asti, where at the age of 10 he began studying piano at the Giuseppe Verdi Music Institute under the guidance of organist and composer Giuseppe Peirolo, later moving to the Antonio Vivaldi Conservatory in Alessandria, a city 37km due east of Asti, to continue his studies with the concert pianist Maria Gachet.He gave up a career in music and instead trained to become a doctor, and continues to practise medicine in his home city to this day. In 2012, AltRock released a Locanda delle Fate CD of tracks written at the same time as but not included on Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi�, recorded by the 2010 incarnation of the band and supplemented with excerpts from a gig at Asti's Teatro Alfieri on November 21st 1977, a performance which does include Conta.In one of the most unbelievable examples of sampling (even stranger than 50 Cent using Me and You for Other Days from I Pooh's 1973 album Parsifal for his song Everytime I Come Around), rapper/producer Dr. Dre used Conta's piano arpeggio from Vendesi Saggezza throughout For The Love of Money on the 2015 CD Compton, which was nominated for Best Rap Album at the 2015 Grammy Awards; the film Straight Outta Compton inspired by the CD was also nominated for the best screenplay at the Oscars. It should be said that Conta has been recognised as the copyright holder.Conta's love of music remained and he continued to compose, eventually deciding to record some of the compositions with the help of the sound engineer and co-arranger Simone Lampedone. The CD Endless Nights was released on AMS records in 2019, a collection of original compositions built up since he left the band. He admits it took a long time to complete this album but he has been working as a doctor throughout. Conta has stated that Endless Nights reflects the changes of the last 40-50 years, from the golden age of prog when form and structure in music were important, to the present day with its immediacy and modern music production values. When you first hear the instrumental � nell'aria (It's in the Air) you're transported back to 1977, with the piano melody and the staccato guitar phrasing providing a sonic link to A Volte un Istante di Quiete. The track also provides an insight into the quality of his collaborators, with Gavin Harrison (Porcupine Tree, King Crimson) on drums.With You on the Walk of my Life has a similar feel and is of a very similar length to � nell'aria though this track features vocals, delivered by guitarist Ermanno Brignolo and sung in English. There's more synthesizer, but still lots of gorgeous piano.Notte Infinita (title track Endless Nights) is another instrumental, but this provides a degree of contrast because it has a more modern sounding palette, with synthesizer given more of a lead role. The song builds up following a choral keyboard section, slows briefly before resuming the up-tempo, uplifting feel with guitar and synthesizer sharing the melody.Growin' Up is another track with a distinctive Costa-penned melody line reminiscent of Locanda delle Fate and lots more piano. The arrangement varies between modern sounding during the vocal passages, sung in English, and a structure reflecting his writing in the 70s. In Riva Al Mondo (On the Shores of the World) is sung in Italian. Beginning with tolling bells, it's played at a slower tempo with acoustic guitar, lending a prog-romantic feeling. The keyboard work is primarily piano lead and the whole piece is much more orchestrated. The pace is picked up around the middle of the track, and there's some restrained electric guitar before the tempo moves down a gear for another vocal section, then picks up again before slowing and fading.Fiori Nascoti (Hidden Flowers) begins with piano and cello, a reflective orchestral introduction followed by a modern sounding break, before the melody is introduced and rather like the preceding track, the pace increases and slows as layers of instruments are added and subtracted. The vocals are short and at the very end of the piece, which ends with a piano flourish.Overall, the album is uplifting, positive-sounding and has a brightness that's difficult to define. The beautiful piano playing provides a link back to Locanda delle Fate and I'd recommend this album to any fan of Forse Le Lucciole Non Si Amano Pi�, but Endless Nights manages to occupy territory shared with modern progressivo italiano acts. It doesn't sound like a solo album either, because the songs have been sympathetically arranged for the different musicians and their respective instruments. It may have taken a long time to make, but it was most definitely worth it.An easy 4 stars

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — ASCETA, the "ascetic ones" have emerged from their chamber prog hideaway somewhere in the the regionof the greater Santiago metroplex in Chile only to unleash their third lauded release THE FOOLLEADING THE BLIND which continues their uncanny ability to channel their inner Univers Zero, ArtZoyd, Rational Diet and other prerequisite classic chamber music oriented RIO acts that have keptthe musical underground electrified for the past half century. As an octet of classically trainedmusicians undergoing Cirque du Soleil musical acrobatics, this band weaves a conceptual tale offalse leadership through mass manipulation in an all-instrumental processions of classic avant-prog,chamber rock and avant-garde angularity. The album opens with the band's most energized and ambitious effort yet, the 21 1/2 minute titletrack which tackles the classic prog excesses in full dynamics. A versatile enigmatic excursionthrough a never-ending labyrinthine maze of motifs and crafty cadences, ASCETA goes for the progjugular right from the get go which continues the band's amazing display of instrumental interplaysounding like a seasoned symphony that has been in existence for decades but in actuality only amere six years in the making. With epic grandeur and bassoon-backed blazing bravado the title trackcatapults ASCETA to the top ranks of modern chamber prog, an exhilarating entryway to the band'sthird offering but also a bit of a false climatic start as it steals the thunder from the rest ofthe album's playlist.Although it swallows up nearly half of THE FOOL LEADING THE BLIND's playing time of 53 minutes, thetrack finally cedes to the following "Temple Of Mirrors" which offers a mesmerizing shorter arrayof twisted melodic constructs along with rock guitar grittiness and eccentric time signature changesrun amok, the quintessence of wily crazy complex prog along with dark and angsty atmospheres. "WhenThey Arrive" serves as the album's, uh ballad perhaps? A slow eerie and oozing instrumentalpowerhouse that remains true to the complexities of the album's true nature albeit with a touch ofmelancholic surrender. "Everything Stopped" on the other hand delivers a more bombastic introfollowed by a phantasmic slower procession of alternating instrumentation that has been compared toa cinematic score that offers an intensity that deserves some sort of visual counterpart. The albumends with the 10-minute closer "Momento Mori" which offers some of the strongest polyrhythms andavant-prog excess.Another strong album by one of South America's most dedicated chamber prog acts on par quality withthe greatest since the advent of the style's hybridizing effects that were spawned by the greatHenry Cow. An active album indeed as an inattentive listening session may result in jet lag howevercareful dedication to the procession of sounds that emerge will result in a most satisfying displayof modern avant-chamber prog in the finest of forms. If any complaints are to be made, i guess itfeels that ASCETA is very much going through the motions as traditionalists rather than offeringsome new stylistic rejuvenation and as mentioned, the title track seems to usurp the remainingalbum's intensity however despite a few nitpicking quirks that keep it from perfection, ASCETAcontinues to generate some of the most brilliant doses of this musical style since Rational Dietfolded in 2010. Add to that the entire concept thing seems a bit contrived as it seems like a progcheck list feature that really has no relevance to this music that seems to meander wherever itfeels. Nevertheless, amazing musicianship and captivating music.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Anneke Van Giersbergen launches her second LP with a powerful sense of grief, a song about life before love."Fade In Fade Out" features flawless piano and vocals, a contained explosion of folk-rock-pop reminiscent of The Gathering with its rich synths. The latent break, a fierce, chaotic, progressive riff, is punctuated by a captivating saxophone in a dreamlike crescendo. An acoustic reprise showcases her inimitable voice as a ballad over a Southern-tinged guitar. "Handle Me With Care" boasts an electro beat, reminiscent of The Corrs, The Cranberries, and Blondie, with its distinctive drums; a minimalist new-wave pop sound. The saxophone returns, accompanied by a synth on Ultravox in a binary, danceable, and solemn mode."Red Sky" stands out for its perfect harmony between the phrased vocals and the minimalist instrumental, reminiscent of The White Stripes. The synth bass reminiscent of the Smashing Pumpkins evokes the 90s. Anneke drifts along without a care in the world, accompanied by a subtly lush orchestration, culminating in a bewitching, mantra-like folk vocal finale. "Sail Towards The Sun," a melancholic, poignant acoustic ballad brimming with emotion, recounts her farewell to her father and memories of sailing trips; drums and classical instruments accompany her angelic voice.Anneke van Giersbergen continues to showcase her angelic voice on this second installment of her triptych chronicling the loss of her parents.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Rodrigo San Mart�n is mostly known as an argentinian niche, musician oriented content creator, hehas a decent presence on the community and has, alongside bands like Qu�sar (which I've reviewedpreviously) organized progressive rock festivals in the recent years, he's a relevant figure in theargentinian underground scene although his music remains relatively obscure, he currently works as amusic teacher.He's had a LOT of projects both solo and band oriented, and as he himself has stated, for a while heleft music and composed only to himself, due to the lack of commercial success and recognition,which is a sad assessment of the reach and interest of the general public on prog rock. Still hiswork remains high quality and interesting, this, "Otro d�a en la distop�a" is his latest LP release,it dwells on relevant topics ranging from surveillance states, algorithmic numbness, the destructionof communities and life after the pandemic...therefore, it *will be a strongly emotional album*.As it is my tradition, I would like to start off by dissecting the quality of the compositionsthemselves, which, is quite consistent throughout the entirety of the album's run-time. The range ofthe compositions oscillates between two (theoretically as in practice it *works*) opposing forces :Heavy, energetic and aggressive vs emotional, quiet and intimate music. These 2 blocks are bestrepresented by the 2 opening tracks, "Las palabras que negu�" (a track that opens and closes thealbum as it's split in two parts, just as "Shine on you crazy diamond" and "The sky moves sideways"were) is by far the album's emotional core, intimate, slow and deliberately tension-building, thetrack relies on a piano and guitar leitmotifs alongside sensitive, jazz, tango and ballad likerhythms overlaped with ambient textures, the track builds tension that is released with a swirlingand bluesy guitar solo, a feeling which inspires images of cozy blankets on an otherwise bad day, itresembles Pink Floyd and Porcupine tree's early works (I didn't mention them just as a fun fact!)and the small acoustic moments are like the golden hour, this bloc of (mellow) songs can beinterpreted as representations of a decaying humanity and the mental health crisis we are currentlyexperiencing as a society. On the other bloc, the title track "Otro d�a en la distop�a" is heavy,flute leaning (very akin to bands like Jethro Tull and Spanish band M�go de �z) and has a hightempo, aggressive playing and lots of distortion, with a slower paced yet still as energetic chorusthat has a mellotron in it, it represents the aggressive most machine like side of modern society...despite that, I consider the actual heavy song of the album is "La mirada que devuelve el reflejo"which has an absolute killer riff. Overall, the compositions are all very interesting and consistentin quality, each one is creative and takes a spin on already established music tendencies,therefore, despite being progressive, they are actually quite easy to digest, this recalls an auraof bands like argentinian group "Sui generis", and Spanish bands "Extremoduro" and "Asfalto", everysingle track is quite enjoyable and they all keep the same emotional core which is an aura ofnumbness, loss, confusion, fear and paranoia, I could definitely picture myself reading HoracioQuiroga's works (yes I know he's Uruguayan but still) to the instrumental sections of the record.Without getting too much into the production, I can say it's crystal clear, this is incredibleconsidering the fact that, after all, this is a record that was recorded, mixed and mastered on ahome studio, settings like that don't usually end up making gourmet production but this isn't thecase, granted San Mart�n is both as technically formed an engineer and a musician. You can feel theweight and dread of every instrument and the pitches hit precisely in tune, the way the layers arearranged and programmed on the Bandcamp software is milimetrically precise, nothing is ever off abeat, the mixing is great although I could actually enjoy the album a little more if the bass wasmore audible and there's no problems like reverberation, feedback, bloated audio etc. For being aone man project, the production is as precise as if it were done by a team of professionals on agreat studio.Now...not everything is sunshine, lollipops and rainbows, this album has two fatal flaws thatseverely hurt the experience and lower the quality of the record overall, these two flaws being thelyrics and the vocals.I'll start with the vocals...and I'd like to compare it to the situation of Rush's early records,remember how Geddy Lee used to sign obnoxiously high pitched, like he wasn't breathing and superrough? Yeah that also sums up the situation of the vocals here perfectly. San Mart�n attempts tosing WAY higher than his actual vocal range and tries to keep his voice soft and heartfelt, thesetwo end up turning into a negative feedback and they both end up harming the record. His voice isdifficult to listen through most of the records, specially in those moments where he adds littlechoruses and secondary vocal lines, eclipsing the wonderful instrumentals with rough vocals. Attimes this can make you even want to stop listening to the record all together since it is so onyour face and difficult to dismiss, taking into account that San Mart�n is a professional, skilledmusician, this is also contradictory to his training, and is something he could actually improve. (As a side note, his new band "Auguria" released a single around 2 months ago, where anothervocalist is doing the singing and that only shows how prominent this problem is on his own soloworks [despite the single not being great either])The lyrics are also quite poor, despite dealing with visceral, relevant and deeply polemic topicsrelated to our new status quo, something which should result in string lyrics, they are very cliche,hollow and amateurish, not nearly as polished compared to other contemporary Hispanic bands of thisday and era like Chilean band Hesse Kassel, nor do they live up to San Mart�n's inspirations such asRoger Waters. They don't really do justice to the topics, and explore them so dimly and on such asurface level, non metaphoric ("I don't want to be one's and zero's, really? We're talking about a compatriot of Benedetti, Cort�zar and Borges...come on) way that they are not a good piece of poetry by any means. Add this tomy previous critique to the records vocals and you'll understand why I say this significantlyhinders the experience you can get out of this album.Overall, it's an album of mixed quality, technically and musically impressive but weak lyrically andthus, emotionally (as lyrics are what's most important to emotions in concept albums, with theexception of adaptations to literary works such as camel's "The snow goose"), it's something I'drecommend to symphonic rock fans but adding the nuance of it's strong downsides, it's an enjoyable record despite it's flaws, instrumentally wonderful, weak on concept execution and lyrics...it's a piece of art that will resonate more with those who value instrumentation over lyrics.

items.body: Alina Ibragimova and Cédric Tiberghien have returned to Beethoven‘s violin sonatas, this time performing exclusively on period instruments. Having previously recorded the complete cycle on modern instruments for the Wigmore Hall Live label, the duo opens this new project with the three Op. 12 sonatas and the Spring Sonata (No. 5). Ibragimova plays a c. 1775 Anselmo Bellosio violin, while Tiberghien performs on a Paul McNulty fortepiano modeled after a 1794 Anton Walter instrument. Walter was a premier maker whose fortepianos were favored by both Mozart and Beethoven, making this an ideal historical match for the repertoire. Violin Sonatas Vol. 1 Amazon Presto Apple In the Violin Sonata No. 1 in D Major, Op. 12 No. 1, the duo immediately establishes a standard of precision. The Allegro con brio is immaculate in its synchronicity and articulation, from the neatly truncated phrasing of the opening bars to the clarity of the rolling arpeggios. Despite this exacting attention to detail, the quintessential Beethovenian spirit of contrast and surprise remains fully intact; the musicians grasp the raw vitality of one moment and juxtapose it with grace and lyricism in the next. While the period instruments may not possess the powerful, rounded polish of their modern counterparts, their rawness imparts a distinct and memorable flavor. The slightly rough-around-the-edges timbre and scrappy enthusiasm only heighten the sense of authenticity in the performance. The middle movement, a theme and variations, is arguably the most emotionally eclectic section of the sonata, and the duo wastes no time exploring the character of each variation. The theme evokes the charm of a Mozart minuet, giving way to a graceful dialogue between violin and piano in the subsequent variations. As the music gathers momentum, the violin assumes an increasingly pleading tone that heightens the tension. The minor variation at the 3’48” mark is where true Beethovenian drama makes its entrance. Tiberghien and Ibragimova wholeheartedly embrace the stormy intensity, with the fortepiano providing a convincing rumble in its bass register. Of the other two sonatas in the Op. 12 set, No. 3 in E-flat Major calls to mind the Eroica symphony, not just due to the shared key, but also in its regal character. Here, the duo taps into another dimension of their artistry: the ability to create a convincing orchestral profile. The Allegro con spirito presents a noble and stately personality, while the Rondo adds a more assertive, rhythmic drive. The relative lightness of the period instruments in no way inhibits the players from generating a resplendent, full-bodied tone. The Sonata No. 2 in A Major follows and serves as the most playful, yet virtuosic, offering on the program. In the Allegro vivace, the duo brings humor and persistence to the inquisitive two-note phrases, but it is the meticulous, effortless-sounding passagework that truly stands out. This whimsical energy establishes a striking contrast with the middle movement, the only one on the album set in a minor key. Tiberghien and Ibragimova seize this rare moment of melancholy to deliver a tender, sensitive reading of real gravity. Cédric Tiberghien and Alina Ibragimova. For the Spring Sonata, the duo makes the most of the qualities of their period instruments to present a zesty, energized interpretation. A side-by-side comparison with their previous modern-instrument recording reveals pointed differences. While certain interpretive mannerisms remain — such as Tiberghien’s rubato in the piano part or Ibragimova’s crisp bowing and tight rhythms — the modern version feels warmer, mellower, and heavier, largely due to the modern piano’s resonance. Conversely, the period recording feels perfectly fitted to the idyllic, refreshing spirit of the sonata. Throughout the Allegro assai, Tiberghien displays fine control over phrase contouring. The tone of a fortepiano can often feel fleeting, yet he manages to create grounded, distinct closures to his phrases, alongside finely graded softer dynamics. Ibragimova matches this level of musicianship, offering a wide range of timbral characters. Her violin can drop to barely a whisper, yet quickly pivot to a much more adamant profile during robust passages. A minor gripe is that the violin occasionally overpowers the piano, though this may be more a matter of microphone placement than musical balance. The slow movement provides a glimpse into the opposite end of the emotional spectrum, replacing bubbling energy with a deeply satisfying calm. Once again, the period instruments lend an added angle of translucence and fragility rarely heard on modern recordings. The duo is superbly matched here, with Ibragimova providing a supportive, sensitive backdrop during the piano’s melodic lines. Richard Wigmore’s accompanying liner notes offer helpful stylistic analysis and commentary on the sonatas’ connections to other works in Beethoven’s catalogue. Ultimately, Tiberghien and Ibragimova prove fully at home in the period-instrument domain, delivering performances of real dimension and personality. Should you buy this album if you already own the previous cycle by the duo? The answer is yes, and certainly if you are looking for what promises to be a first-class period-instrument cycle of Beethoven’s complete violin sonatas. items.body: Any album that sounds as though everybody involved remembered to wipe their feet before entering the studio should probably be regarded with suspicion. Fortunately, Wailin Storms’ The Arsonist sounds more like four people discovered a door already hanging crooked from its hinges and decided the sensible course was to make the room less structurally sound. The Durham band carries the American South around like a family curse, hauling blues, gothic rock, punk, doom, Baptist hymns and old folk dread into the same cramped quarters. Their fifth album, and first for Season of Mist, was recorded fully analogue by Matt Talbott of Hum, an appropriate choice for music that benefits from scraped edges and human error. Justin Storms wanted portions of the record to reconnect with the primitive four-track character of the band’s beginnings. “Some of these songs are more primitive and stripped down, hearkening back to the four-track recordings that the band started with,” says Storms. “The recordings contain flaws, but remain human in all the right ways. They could be a murder ballad or an old folk song that’s sung around the campfire.” Standout track Dead End provides an appropriately diseased introduction. Ben Melton’s guitar worries at Steve Stanczyk’s bass while Mark Oates pounds out a rhythm that seems increasingly annoyed about being alive. There is some Radiohead in its queasy grandeur, the poetic ecstasy of The Doors’ Jim Morrison, and plenty of The Gun Club in its bloodshot blues logic. Then Storms sings “Calm night / Birds keep plucking out our eyes” with the casual authority of a man reporting local traffic conditions. Fire has followed Storms since childhood, when his fascination with flames nearly resulted in the destruction of his family home. Here it becomes appetite, catastrophe, sex, faith and bad judgment sharing one cigarette. Flannery O’Connor would recognize the neighborhood immediately: everybody has dressed for church, salvation is theoretically available, and somebody somewhere has misplaced a can of gasoline. You Never Answered turns the miserable modern habit of staring into a phone into a deafening plea for actual contact. Elsewhere, war and ordinary social machinery feed the record’s agitation before the title track slows everything into a bruised procession. Love suddenly becomes another uncontrollable force capable of rearranging a life without requesting permission. Never Rest swells into a crescendo of horror as it unfurls a wild torrent of haunting poetry set against apocalyptic guitars and thundering drums – landing somewhere between Type O Negative and The Doors. The Arsonist finds Wailin Storms standing dangerously close to their oldest impulses: primitive rock & roll, folk horror, damaged romance and the suspicion that salvation and catastrophe may share an address. items.body: Never mess with Murdoch’s society Crashing and burning oh what a pity Tracky Nike fourth reich vitriol spray Commonplace everyday wreck of the UK Modern life has become one long argument with a screen, a boss, a stranger, a lover, or the idiot currently screaming beneath a flag in a supermarket car park. Shaven Primates have mined the exhaustion and alchemized it into a new EP, Kill The Algorithm. The Oxford quartet turns private dependency, political resentment, male grievance, and algorithmic manipulation into four rough-and-tumble songs powered by post-punk tension, industrial abrasion, art-rock unease, and guitars that sound ready to put somebody through a wall. Saviour starts from the most private wound. Its language treats affection as narcotic relief, the beloved transformed into medicine for absences that began much earlier, somewhere around the missing mother, missing father, and the suspicion that another person might finally close the hole. The 1990s references make sense: Placebo’s bruised glamour, Nine Inch Nails’ compulsive machinery, A Perfect Circle’s heavy-lidded grandeur. The emotional centre remains ugly enough to feel dangerous. Love becomes dosage, fantasy becomes diagnosis, and the repeated appeal to a saviour keeps curdling into evidence that salvation has been outsourced to somebody equally mortal. Pioneer Way drags that anxiety into public, where the nervous breakdown has flags tied to the lamp posts. The track takes aim at a Britain of workplace exhaustion, tabloid conditioning, immigrant scapegoating, screen addiction, and everyday fury looking for a body to blame. There is something grimly comic about a man screaming at an indicator while the country around him rehearses imperial fantasies beside a roundabout. The Sex Pistols influence is less about imitation than permission: permission to sneer at the pageantry, to notice how easily personal failure gets repackaged as national grievance, and to turn the resulting disgust into a hook sharp enough to draw blood. Then Feed goes after the salesmen. These are the grievance merchants who discover lonely young men, tell them tenderness is weakness, sell coercion as confidence, and monetize every insecurity they helped aggravate. The band brings in the clenched attack of Rage Against the Machine and Metallica, but the song’s ugliest idea is economic. Misery has become a business model. The customer is kept hungry because a satisfied customer might stop clicking. That thought detonates fully in Kill The Algorithm, where social media becomes less a tool than a delivery system for appetite, paranoia, tribal identity, and manufactured certainty. Radiohead, Black Sabbath and Iron Maiden hover in the architecture, while the repeated command at the song’s centre turns disgust into something nearly ecstatic. The target is the machine that keeps learning which wound to prod next. Listen to Kill The Algorithm below: Shaven Primates have made four songs about dependence: on lovers, on screens, on enemies, on gurus, on systems that promise relief while feeding the sickness. The riffs grind, the drums hit with factory-floor force, and the vocals move from wounded croon to open-throated accusation. The EP is held together by the recognition that private desperation and public brutality are often roommates, splitting the rent while each insists the other started the fire. items.body: German post-punk and darkwave act Escape With Romeo released their 13th studio album, “Night After Night”, on August 7, 2026 through Zeitklang. The Cologne band’s new release arrives on CD digipak and digital, and follows the group’s 2024 comeback album “Suspicious Bliss”. Night After Night by Escape With Romeo ‘Night After Night’ tracklist and credits “Night After Night” runs 14 tracks: “Edit Me Out”, “No Turning Back”, “Sound and the Fury”, “Something That Lasts”, “New World Order”, “Cancel Anytime”, “I Need Something Stronger”, “Fear’s a Ghost”, “Little Did I Know”, “Night After Night”, “Skyscraper Spiders”, “I’m My Own Worst Enemy”, “You Need the Drugs” and “Wrong Side of Town Pt. 2”. All songs are written by singer, guitarist and songwriter Thomas Elbern, except “You Need the Drugs”, a cover of the 2013 WestBam track featuring Richard Butler of the Psychedelic Furs, credited here to its writers Klaus Jankuhn, Maximilian Lenz and Butler. The album was recorded, mixed and produced by Elbern and drummer Frenzy Erl at Zeitklang in Brühl and Highline in Munich between January 2025 and June 2026, and mastered by Erl. Elbern handles vocals, guitars, synths, vocoder and samples, with Frenzy Erl on drums, Tobias Schwartz on bass and Stella Tonon on vocals. Artwork and graphic design are by schmalfett.com. Themes and rollout The band describes “Night After Night” as harder, more emotional and more direct than “Suspicious Bliss”, the direction Elbern set out to push further at the start of 2025. Songs including “No Turning Back” and “New World Order” address what the band calls a dystopian zeitgeist shaped by AI, while “Skyscraper Spiders” and “Wrong Side of Town Pt. 2” extend the mood signalled by the single “Fear’s a Ghost”. Press materials for the release describe it as “somewhere between post-rock, trip-hop, and the much overused term post-punk.” “Night After Night” was preceded by the singles “Fear’s a Ghost”, released on February 6, 2026, and “Sound and the Fury”, which Side-Line covered as the third single from the album in March 2026. The band will support the album with a Germany tour in autumn 2026, performing as a trio and mixing songs from “Night After Night” with material from across its history. About Escape With Romeo Escape With Romeo was founded in Cologne in 1989 by singer and guitarist Thomas Elbern, who had previously fronted the new wave band Seltsame Zustände and played guitar and wrote songs for Pink Turns Blue. The band’s early catalog appeared through Sound Factory, starting with the self-titled “Escape With Romeo” in 1990 and continuing with “Autumn on Venus” (1991), “Next Stop Eternally” (1993), “Blast of Silence” (1996) and “How Far Can You Go” (1998), a run that included the early single “Somebody”, the band’s best-known track from that period. Keyboardist Martin Pott joined from the second album onward. From 2001 the band’s releases moved to Zeitklang, the label Elbern runs himself, starting with “Come Here White Light” (2001) and continuing through “Love Alchemy” (2002), “Psalms of Survival” (2004), “Emotional Iceage” (2007), “Samsara” (2012) and “After the Future” (2015). Escape With Romeo announced its farewell in 2017, played a final tour in 2018 and had dissolved following festival appearances in 2019. The band returned in 2022 with the double compilation “Based on a True Story – Best of Escape With Romeo”, which led into “Suspicious Bliss”, released on November 1, 2024 as the first new studio album since “After the Future”. The 2026 rollout for “Night After Night” opened with “Fear’s a Ghost” in February, followed by “Sound and the Fury” in March, and now arrives with the album itself on August 7, 2026 via Zeitklang.

items.body: Dead Can Dance released the album “Anastasis” on 13 August 2012 through PIAS Recordings. The eighth studio album by the British-Australian duo Brendan Perry and Lisa Gerrard turns 14 this year. It was their first studio release in 16 years, following 1996’s “Spiritchaser,” and their first album not released on 4AD. Dead Can Dance separated in 1998 while working on a follow-up to “Spiritchaser,” cancelling the album and an accompanying tour. The duo reunited in 2005 for a 31-date world tour that did not produce new studio material. Perry announced in May 2011 that the band would record a new album and return to touring. “Anastasis” and a full world tour were confirmed together in 2012, with the tour opening in Canada days ahead of the album’s release and running into July 2013. “Anastasis” contains eight tracks: “Children of the Sun,” “Anabasis,” “Agape,” “Amnesia,” “Kiko,” “Opium,” “Return of the She-King” and “All in Good Time,” with a total running time of 56 minutes. Dead Can Dance wrote, performed and produced the album themselves; Aidan Foley handled mastering. The title is the Greek word for resurrection. “Anastasis” reached number 8 on the UK Albums Chart and number 9 on the US Billboard World Albums chart, and was certified double gold by the Independent Music Companies Association in 2014 for sales of at least 150,000 copies across Europe. Anastasis by Dead Can Dance About Dead Can Dance Dead Can Dance formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1981 as a trio of Brendan Perry, Paul Erikson and Simon Monroe, with Lisa Gerrard joining shortly after on vocals and percussion. The band relocated to London in 1982 and signed to 4AD, releasing its self-titled debut album on 27 February 1984. Six further studio albums followed on 4AD through the 1980s and 1990s: “Spleen and Ideal” (1985), “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” (1987), “The Serpent’s Egg” (1988), “Aion” (1990), “Into the Labyrinth” (1993) and “Spiritchaser” (1996). Perry and Gerrard disbanded the project in 1998 during sessions for a planned follow-up to “Spiritchaser,” which was never completed under that title. A reunion tour followed in 2005, taking in 31 shows across Europe and North America, including performances at the Hollywood Bowl and Radio City Music Hall backed by 40-piece orchestras. In May 2011, Perry announced through his official channels that Dead Can Dance would record new material and tour again. That work led to “Anastasis,” released via PIAS Recordings on 13 August 2012 as the band’s first album away from 4AD. Dead Can Dance followed it with “Dionysus” on PIAS Recordings in 2018, its most recent studio album to date.

items.body: Although Dirk Serries may have retired the Vidna Obmana moniker years ago, albums continue to be released under the name. While these are usually reissues or live recordings, this particular series is generating significant interest. The third installment in the “Twilight Of Perception Redux” series compiles rare and previously unreleased recordings from the Belgian project’s archives, spanning the years 1996 to 2006. The three CDs contain a total of 18 tracks, no fewer than 13 of which fall into the category of—let’s call them—‘curiosities’. Each disc features six tracks that immediately draw the listener into Vidna Obmana’s unique world. These are long, elaborate compositions characterized by generally slow, tribal rhythms that merge with deep, astral, and dreamlike soundscapes. Dirk Serries’ universe evokes a sense of mystery—and at times, a certain darkness—accentuated by field recordings and various forms of sound manipulation. At times, you feel as though you are wandering through a labyrinth of crystalline sounds; moments later, you are drawn towards an imaginary black hole, only to undergo an almost abyssal experience on the next track. Occasionally, a guitar emerges, played in an Ambient style that adds a touch of diversity to the overall atmosphere. Vidna Obmana was a project that fused different styles into a unique whole—a universe where Tribal and Ambient music formed a symbiotic relationship, sweeping the listener away into an imaginative world of richness, even on the darker tracks. This album is a perfect addition to the Vidna Obmana discography for many enthusiasts. Even decades after their creation, these tracks retain an irresistible allure—like a forbidden space where you simply have to discover what is unfolding inside. (Rating:8). Listen to “Threshold Of Obstruction”: Threshold Of Obstruction by Vidna Obmana About Vidna Obmana Vidna Obmana is the pseudonym of Belgian composer Dirk Serries, born in 1968. Serries recorded as Vidna Obmana from 1984 until 2007, when he officially retired the name, moving his active work to the Fear Falls Burning project. The name is Serbian for “optical illusion”. Working in Ambient, Minimal and Drone music, Serries released albums through labels including ND Records, Hypnos Recordings, Soleilmoon Recordings and Projekt Records, and collaborated with artists such as Steve Roach, Asmus Tietchens and Bass Communion. The original “Twilight Of Perception” appeared on Projekt in 1997. “Twilight Of Perception Redux Volume Three 1996 – 2006” compiles archival recordings from that period on Zoharum.

items.body: The continuing solo adventures of Elkhorn’s Drew Gardner find the NY-based artist following the groove and exploring within it thoroughly with an expert crew of free improv players skilled in the ways of aural psychedelics. Freshly unleashed by Eiderdown Records, Rabbit Ears rips through juggernaut acid rockers (such as the thunderous title cut that opens the record with a major BANG), slithering dual guitar chases (“Holmdel Horn Antenna” and “Garden Eels”) and drifting meditative soundscapes (“Conch Shell”). With Tom Malach on second guitar and Andy Cush on bass (both from Garcia Peoples) and Ryan Jewell on drums (from…well, nearly everything we cover here on RCU), Gardner plays with a patient looseness born of utter trust in his collaborators while navigating the cosmic waves of prismatic sounds that surge throughout each track. This familiarity and freedom allows for the band’s synergy to bloom into confident, fully kaleidoscopic jams. Each piece glows with a palpable excitement with each musician bringing their absolute best to the table, creating a tight and cohesive supergroup sound (minus the ego!) that would be more fitting for a band ten times their age. With red-hot wah-wah fuzz, bombastic rhythms and an overall mellow yet doomy atmosphere, this is an instant psych-rock classic that even Hendrix himself would have dug. Be sure to grab your copy from Eiderdown on vinyl or digital today. -KH

ペルトコスキ＆トゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管 日本ツアーへ発つ直前の舞台 2025／26シーズン末のフィルハーモニー・ド・パリには、フィンランドの優れた教授ヨルマ・パヌラ門下の若手二人があいついで指揮台に立った。 26歳のタルモ・ペルトコスキは2024年からトゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管弦楽団の音楽監督を務めている。本拠地トゥールーズの演奏に続いたパリ公演は、成功裡に終わった日本ツアーへ出発する直前の6月2日に行われた。 前半はアレクサンドル・カントロフを迎えてのベートーヴェン「ピアノ協奏曲第4番」ト長調だった。冒頭の第1主題から、カントロフのピアノは、ソロ楽器の即興性から生まれる華やかさと、作曲家が曲に託した心情を音に込めた内省的な側面の双方を兼ね備えていた。その印象は全3楽章を通じて変わらなかったが、この二面性が実現された大きな要因はピアノ独奏を最大限に尊重した指揮にあった。 自身もピアニストであるペルトコスキは、オーケストラを常に安定したテンポに保つことにより、ソリストの自由を最大限に広げた。阿吽の呼吸によって、苛烈さと優しい抒情が鮮やかに音となって広がっていった。この間、一度としてピアニストのほうに視線を向けなかったことは、この指揮者の耳が破格であることの証左であろう。 カントロフの演奏そのものが、1台の楽器というよりもオーケストラを思わせるだけに、この組み合わせによって、ベートーヴェンがこの曲に明快に打ち出した「交響作品」という特徴が際立って感じられた。聴き手は、あたかもピアノを伴った交響的幻想曲を前にしているような気持ちにひたされた。 カントロフは現役ピアニストのなかでも傑出したテクニックの持ち主だが、テクニックがあくまでも表現のための手段となっているので、聴いていて鼻につかない。そして彼の手にかかると、曲想は常に自然に流れていく。5曲ある楽聖のピアノ協奏曲のなかで、もっともインティメートな作品が、彼の気性にいちばんピッタリしているのかもしれない。 アンコールは夢を見ているかのようなブラームス「3つの間奏曲」作品117から「第1番」変ホ長調、次いで音符が自在に飛翔するかのようなスクリャービン《焔に向かって》だった。 後半のマーラー「交響曲第6番《悲劇的》」イ短調では、第1楽章の行進曲を思わせる冒頭から、弦楽器の音量を抑えめにして、全4楽章を通じて感情を抑制した演奏となった。音色の多彩さと細部に留意した指揮によって、トゥールーズ・キャピトル国立管の華やかな管楽器群のソロが前面に出た。 前半の一部において緊迫感がやや低下した箇所があったにせよ、第3楽章アンダンテから第4楽章フィナーレにかけてのドラマの高揚感は誰にも抗しがたかった。指揮者に対する団員の信頼は絶大で、壮大な曲が終わると、観客に負けない拍手が舞台の上に湧き上がった。 パリ管がマケラ指揮、ファウストの独奏で28年ぶりにシューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」 シューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」が終わって、拍手に応えるイザベル・ファウスト（中央左）とクラウス・マケラ（中央右）© 三光 洋 6月10日には、パリで圧倒的な人気を誇るクラウス・マケラがパリ管弦楽団を指揮した。 シューマン「ヴァイオリン協奏曲」ニ短調は名ヴァイオリニスト、ヨーゼフ・ヨアヒムのために1853年秋に一気に書かれた。しかし、ヨアヒムが「弾くのが難しく、舞台映えしない」という理由を挙げて演奏しなかっただけでなく、総譜の出版も差し止めてしまった。作曲家は生前に耳にすることができず、初演されたのはナチス時代の1937年になってからといういわくつきの作品である。パリ管が取り上げるのも、1998年以来28年ぶりの2度目で、きわめてまれだ。 イザベル・ファウストは楽譜を見つめながら、細やかな感受性を反映したよどみのない輝きのある演奏により、高貴なシューマンの世界へと聴き手を導いてくれた。マケラの指揮も優しくソリストを包み込む繊細なものだった。 最後の「幻想序曲《ロメオとジュリエット》」は、シェイクスピア劇の数場面をチャイコフスキーが卓越したドラマ感覚により音にしている。リムスキー=コルサコフが「ロシア音楽でもっとも美しい」と絶賛した、コールアングレとヴィオラによる「愛の主題」はとくに名高い。エネルギーの横溢したマケラの指揮に鼓舞されて一体となったパリ管の奏者たちによって、二人の恋人たちの燃え上がる情念がほとばしり、華やいだシーズン閉幕となった。

このとき筆者も現場で音を聴いていたが「何十回も聴いて知っているはずの名曲に、まだこんな発見があるのか」と驚かされた。その要因はいくつかあるが、まずは会場（晴れたら空に豆まいて）のサウンドシステムが抜群のポテンシャルを保持していること。加えて重要なのは、使用する音源の性質である。あのとき、小川氏をはじめ観客を唖然とさせた「音」の正体は何だったのか。そして今回はどんなセッティングでプレイするのか。オノセイゲン氏が語る。 「当日かける音源は、ここでしか聴けない門外不出のDSD（※１）です。これまでマイルスのアルバムはいろんなフォーマットで発売されてきましたが、1999年頃からスーパーオーディオCDで発売されたシリーズがあるんです。これをSACDプレイヤー（エソテリック／K-05XDとG-05）で再生し、さらにSDLab（※2）でカスタムメイドのEQでリマスタリングしました。プラグインなどのデジタル信号処理はしていません」 ※１：アナログ音声を非常に高い周波数で1bitのデジタル信号に変換する、高音質オーディオの記録方式。 ※２：オノ セイゲン氏が率いるSaidera Paradiso Ltd.（有限会社サイデラ・パラディソ）内で「いい音」（主観と物理）を研究、コンサルティングをおこなうラボ（非公開）。 この音源を、氏は「DJ用の私的リマスタリングDSDデータ」としてライブラリー化してきたという。 「この音源は、僕と小川隆夫さんとソニー・ミュージックレーベルズの渡辺巧さんだけが検討用に保持しているもので、僕または小川隆夫さんのイベント（DJ）やラジオ放送、インターネット放送でかけることはできます。この音源のSACD化の可能性を探るべくミーティングを重ねていますが、奇跡的にパッケージ化がオーソライズされるまで一般の方は聴けません。イベント当日は、そのDSDから選りすぐって、TASCAM のDA-3000 DSDマスターレコーダーで再生します」 ジャズ愛好家の間では、アナログレコードを支持するファンも多いが「作品によってはSACDがアナログ盤を凌駕する」という意見も聞かれる。筆者が前回のイベントで得た “驚きのリスニング体験” もはまさにこれだ。オノ氏が続ける。 「SACDのフォーマット＝DSDの音質は、レコード製作者側から見ても “レコードやCDのような物理的な限界” がない、これから録音する音とまったく同じ音を再生できる初めてのフォーマットと言えます」 さらにこうも語る。 「アナログテープは、録音すると若干のヒスノイズと歪みが加わります。もちろんそれがアナログの “いい音” の要素でもありますが、テープやマシンの調整により音の印象は変わるし、アナログテープは経年劣化もあります。したがってアナログ・マスターテープのクローンとも言えるDSDアーカイブ、SACDがあると安心なのです」 当然ながら、これを再生する環境も重要である。会場となる「晴れたら空に豆まいて」の音響については、ここで細かく解説するまでもない、多くの専門家たちが賛辞を贈る素晴らしいセッティング。オノ氏もその特性を熟知した上で、イベント当日の “最も重要なポイント” を挙げる。 「晴れ豆のMeyer Sound speaker のチューニングは重要です。僕はPAエンジニアもやっていますので、再生に使うスピーカーとそのチューニングはとても気を使います。このMeyer Sound とマイルスのDSD リマスター音源の組み合わせは、ある種、魔力的な感動体験をもたらすはずです」」 ここまで聞くと、このイベントがまるで “マイルスのマニアや音響オタクの集い” のように思われるかもしれないが、そうではない。前回も同様、観客と出演者が気軽に会話するような和やかな雰囲気。音楽ファンが集い、みんなで楽しくマイルス音源を聴いてみよう、という趣旨の催しである。 「まだマイルスを聞いたことない、という人も大歓迎ですし、マイルス音源を聴き込んできた玄人ファンの方々も満足してもらえるはずです。いままで聞こえていなかった繊細なハーモニーや、ベース、キックはこうだったのか！ と目を見張るものがあると思いますよ」 イベント当日の司会・進行は原田潤一（ARBAN / Montreux Jazz Festival Japan CEO）と楠元伸哉（ARBAN 編集長）が務める。なお、開場（18:30）から開演（19:15）の間は、出演者参加の「飲み会タイム」として設定されており、観客と出演者が事前に親睦を深めるという趣向になっている。 【開催概要】 マイルス・デイヴィス生誕100年記念─ トーク＆リスニング・イベント 日時：2026年９月30日（水）開場 18:30／開演 19:15 会場：晴れたら空に豆まいて（渋谷区代官山町20−20 モンシェリー代官山B2） 出演：オノセイゲン／小川隆夫 司会：原田潤一（ARBAN / Montreux Jazz Festival Japan CEO）／楠元伸哉（ARBAN 編集長） 前売り券（¥2000）／当日券（¥2500）ともに＋1ドリンク ¥700 小川隆夫 1950年東京生まれ。音楽ジャーナリスト、整形外科医、ギタリスト。1981-83年、ニューヨーク大学大学院留学中に、アート・ブレイキー、ギル・エヴァンス、デクスター・ゴードン、ウィントン・マルサリスなどのミュージシャンや、マックス・ゴードン（「ヴィレッジ・ヴァンガード」オーナー）、マイケル・カスクーナ（プロデューサー）といった関係者の知遇を得る。帰国後ジャズを中心とした原稿の執筆、インタヴュー、翻訳、イヴェント・プロデュースなどを開始。レコード・プロデューサーとしても多くの作品を制作。『ブルーノートの真実』（東京キララ社）、『証言で綴る日本のジャズ1、2』（駒草出版）、『マイルス・デイヴィスの真実』（講談社＋α文庫）、『マイルス・デイヴィス大事典』『ジャズ超名盤研究1-3』『ビバップ読本 言で綴るジャズ史』『来日ジャズメン全レコーディング 1931-1979 レコードでたどる日本ジャズ発展史』『伝説のライヴ・イン・ジャパン』『レーベルで聴くジャズ名盤（1、Part 2）』『ジャズ・クラブ黄金時代〜NYジャズ日記 1981-1983』（いずれもシンコーミュージック・エンタテイメント）など著書も多数。 オノ セイゲン 1978-80年、音響ハウスに在籍（映写係）。その後フリーランスのPA/録音エンジニアとして、青葉市子、三宅純、坂本龍一、渡辺貞夫、ジョン・ゾーン、マーク・リボウ、アート・リンゼイ、ビル・フリゼール、デヴィッド・シルヴィアン、スティーブ・ジャンセン、オスカー・ピーターソン 、キース・ジャレット、マイルス・デイビスなど多数のアーティストのプロジェクトに参加。 一方で、アーティストとして1984年にJVCよりデビュー、87年に日本人として始めてヴァージンUKと契約する。同年、コム デ ギャルソン 川久保玲氏から「誰も、まだ聴いたことがない音楽を使いたい」「洋服がきれいに見えるような音楽を」という依頼を受けオリジナル楽曲を作曲、制作。『COMME des GARÇONS SEIGEN ONO』はファッション、広告、建築、デザイナーの間でも注目を集める。1993年7月、クロード・ノブスからの招聘によりスイス、モントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバルに４回出演「Montreux 93/94 Seigen Ono Ensemble」などアルバムも多数。サイデラ・レコード主宰。 原田潤一 Montreux Jazz Festival Japan／ARBAN／VISUALNOTES. CEO スイスを本拠地とする世界３大ジャズ・フェスティバル「Montreux Jazz Festival」の日本版「モントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバル・ジャパン」を開催。同フェスではスイスMJFのINTERNATIONAL ADVISORY BOARDメンバーにも名を連ね、日本と欧州の音楽文化を繋ぐ。また、JAZZを中心とする音楽カルチャーメディア「ARBAN」を運営し、大人が楽しめる質の高い音楽情報を日々発信している。 世界を舞台に活躍する作曲家、 三宅純のジャパン・エージェントとしての顔も持ち、NHKドラマの音楽制作などに携わっている。 投稿 最高の音でマイルス作品を聴く─マイルス・デイヴィス生誕100年記念 トーク＆リスニング・イベント “第二弾” 開催決定｜小川隆夫／オノ セイゲンが出演 は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.body: With Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das abruptly change course from the expansive drone works of Meltwater Pulse (2023) and Dragon Rising (2022). The album arrives in violent bursts, assembled from Bangla rap, digital hardcore, dek bass, ambient electronics, and an unusually large network of collaborators stretching from Kolkata to Europe and East Asia. Its premise—a world descending into collective psychosis during the Kali Yuga, inspired in part by Das’s own experience of Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder—could easily have become an exercise in conceptual excess. Instead, organised chaos is built into the record itself. The constant collision of genres, collaborators, and production techniques refuses to settle into a single musical language. From the opening “Schizophrenic Intro”, the listener is thrown into a vortex of slowed-down, sped-up, looped, reversed, and glitched material, with no attempt to ease the transition. The abrasive momentum of “Gondho Jhaater Chule” barely relents in “Escape”, whose spectral vocals provide only the briefest moment of respite before “Iron Age Fantasies” introduces melodic gestures recalling classic Tollywood soundtracks, immediately distorting them into something deeply uncanny. “Laurar Baal” and “Laura Chos” push the collision between noise, Bengali rap, and sampled film dialogue to breaking point, while “E.M.P.” suspends the album inside an extended electronic blackout, one of its most absorbing passages. The unexpected arrival of the Korean gayageum and daegeum (the former a traditional twelve-string plucked zither with a wooden resonating chamber, the latter a large transverse bamboo flute known for its resonant, buzzing tone) on “Cappucc1n0” offers neither resolution nor sentimentality, but a fragile interruption before “Radio Paranoia” and “Maniac Outro” complete the descent into sonic disintegration. The use of crude sexual slang and bodily imagery—particularly in “Gondho Jhaater Chule”, “Laurar Baal”, and “Laura Chos”—adds another layer of instability, grounding the album’s apocalyptic vision in the language of the street as much as in mythology. Vulgarity and transcendence coexist throughout the record, collapsing distinctions between the sacred and the profane with the same ease that it moves between Bangla bass, digital hardcore, ambient electronics, and noise. The density of the album can feel overwhelming at times, and it continually rewires expectations. Yet every stylistic shift destabilises the previous one without feeling arbitrary, reflecting Das’s conception of schizophrenia not as a metaphor but as a lived condition in which disparate realities coexist simultaneously. The album’s many collaborators are given considerable freedom, yet the result never fragments into disconnected contributions; instead, their contrasting vocabularies reinforce the instability at the heart of the project. Challenging but consistently rewarding, Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System places the listener inside the eye of its own sonic vortex, where overload becomes its organising principle rather than an obstacle to it. Corresponding via email, Nilotpal Das sheds further light on the production process. photo by @roh4nlifts at Chandraketugarh Your earlier releases as Bios Contrast—from Dragon Rising and Meltwater Pulse to the forthcoming twelve-hour harmonium drone project under your own name—often revolved around expansive historical, geological, or spiritual concepts explored through long-form composition. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, by contrast, is fragmented, densely collaborative, and rooted in digital hardcore, Bangla rap, experimental electronics, and what you describe as “Brahmancore.” What drew you toward this radically different format? Do you see the album as a departure from your earlier practice, or simply another way of pursuing the same fascination with large-scale conceptual worlds? Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is a very personal album. At the same time, it is a pursuit of a large-scale conceptual world. I wouldn’t say the theme of the album is conceptual, but rather very real. I suffer from Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder, so it’s a take on my worldview. Everything is random and unnecessary but, at the same time, needed, just like the world we live in. People would call me crazy, but I really felt the presence of something godlike, something that controls all of us humans. The album imagines a world descending into mass psychosis during the Kali Yuga, with schizophrenia functioning as both narrative device and sonic metaphor. At the same time, it brings together artists from very different musical and geographical backgrounds—BROOD, Kush Arora, Kim Hae Kyung, Ellery Everet, Seraphim, enesai, P.U.S.Y.E.T.E.R., and many others. How did you coordinate such a diverse group of collaborators while maintaining a coherent dramatic arc? Did each artist respond to a specific chapter in the narrative, or were they encouraged to reinterpret the concept through their own musical language? I didn’t make this album to express or present a very linear story. Every collaborator was free to interpret the concept in their own way. The record is schizophrenic in the sense that it collages many different sounds and genres while maintaining its central theme, which is chaos. And chaos happens naturally while collaborating. At first, I put out an open call for collaborators on Instagram. Many artists quickly DM’d me, and we started a group where we exchanged stems and sounds. Throughout your work you’ve often spoken about “curating sounds” rather than creating something entirely new, drawing on traditional instruments, field recordings, sampling, improvisation, and careful research. On Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, that curatorial approach seems to expand into an entire network of voices, genres, and production methods, from Bangla rap and digital hardcore to ambient passages and Korean traditional instruments. Did working with so many collaborators change your understanding of authorship? At what point does a project of this scale stop feeling like an individual album and become a collective sound world? I started this project with the intention of creating the most mainstream, non-experimental trash music imaginable. The result, however, is the most experimental music I’ve worked on so far. I wasn’t controlling the direction the project was taking; it was a collaborative effort, and it still is. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is also the result of a video game that Kim Hae Kyung is currently developing, called The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System. In an earlier interview you described Kolkata as having only a small experimental music community, while also expressing admiration for artists working across South Asia. Since then, you’ve collaborated with musicians from Europe, North America, East Asia, and beyond, building an unusually international artistic network. Has making Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System changed your perspective on where your music belongs? Do you feel part of a global experimental community now, and how has continuing to work from Kolkata shaped the way you approach collaboration and the exchange of ideas? I would say I don’t belong to an experimental community anymore, but rather to a community that spans many genres, so I fit in with everyone. I like all kinds of music. Kolkata has always had a small experimental community, so I’ve simply accepted that and moved on to other communities. I like mainstream, hard-hitting music now—if the music goes hard, I’m all in, regardless of genre. I have a lot of connections with international artists, and I feel I belong to a global community rather than just a local one, because collaborating is fun, and collaborating with people who have totally different ideas and perspectives is even more fun. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Venetian maestro Gigi Masin, active since the early tape era, threads MIDI phrasing with soft techno patterns and submerged tonal layers. A sense of persistence rather than grief alone Gigi Masin returns with Movement, his first solo LP since Calypso, shifting ambient into pulse-driven structures and sequenced motion. Out on May 29th via Sacred Bones, Movement reframes ambient as physical music, built for shared space, where loops, low frequencies, and sustained tones guide the body as much as the ear. “Deception Dance” has been the first excerpt. This new album is significantly influenced by the recent collaboration with sound designer Rod Modell and also benefits from Anacleto Vitolo’s excellent mastering work. “UMI” and its minimalist style add a touch of coolness that doesn’t feel cold, transporting you to a chill corner of a sweaty room, the same space shared with the seven-and-a-half-minute “Deception Dance,” a minimal techno track that, with snippets of alien-sounding phrases. “Lost,” is dedicated to the disappearance of his wife: an act of love and tenderness conveyed through a synthesized trumpet, representing a “love letter that was no longer received and was thrown into the river.” The more rhythmic tracks (such as “Golden” or ) have been interpreted as a tribute/exploration that blends and reinterprets techno-funk sounds, Balearic bossa nova (in the vein of Manuel Göttsching), and classic Balearic influences. In 2007, the beloved Italian composer lost his entire musical archive in a house flood, forcing him to put music on the back burner for a while. These events could have disrupted his work entirely. Instead, Masin continued to create. The album reflects a sense of persistence rather than grief alone. There is emotion present, but it is expressed through subtle shifts rather than dramatic gestures. Movement is available on Sacred Bones. The prototype instrument has no serial number, but was Vangelis' first CS-80, and was used on his 1977 album Spiral, according to the seller. items.body: Review by yarstruly — This review is simultaneously published on my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights with links and additional information).Enigmatic Sound Machines (ESM) are a collaboration between Jeremie Arrobas (a founding member of Men Without Hats) and Thomas Szirmay (a prog musicologist, researcher, producer, arranger, actor, vocalist and writer). They are based in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. This is their fourth album since their 2023 debut. According to the information I have received, ESM: "is a retro-futuristic project, the brainchild of two childhood friends with a common love for music, philosophy, and the arts." Today I'll be reviewing their 4th album "Divided by One".Over the years, they have expanded to become a 4-piece band. The line-up for this album is as follows.- Jeremie Arrobas/ lead vocals, synth guitars, keyboards, sound machines- Thomas Szirmay /enigmatic voice and sound machines- Alain Bellaiche/ guitars . backing vocals- Hansford Rowe / bass and backing vocalsGuest artists :- Steve Bonino/guitars (1,6)- Roland Buhlmann/ guitars (7)- Anna Arrobas / backing vocals (1,3,4,7)- Laura Piazzai/ lead vocals (8)- Quinn Bachand / violin (8) This album was provided by Anne-Claire Rallo of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Let's listen and find out what all of that means!!Track 1 - Divided by One (6:16)After a few sound effects, a steady drumbeat begins, soon joined by some cool fretless bass work. They lock into a groove, and the guitar plays power chords (Steve Bonino?). Jeramie joins with lead vocals soon after. There is a slight Pink Floyd feel in some ways. The tempo is moderate and the bass part gives it a slightly funky feel. I believe Thomas' "Enigmatic Voice" is in the choruses. I love the overall soundscape. The production is clean and clear. At around 4:30, there are words spoken in what I believe is French. There are some really unique and cool sounds as they begin to bring the song to a close. I really liked that! There are some really different, unique tones, yet it is still accessible to most listeners. And if offering the listener something unique and different isn't progressive, I don't know what is!Track 2 - Chaos Dreaming (9:33)A spooky keyboard sound opens this one. At around 1:20, the rhythm section enters and creates a simple groove. The keyboards and guitar are now playing a melodic motif. About a minute later, the rhythm section temporarily drops out, and they begin a new theme. The vocals come in with the "enigmatic voice". After the 5-minute mark, we get an instrumental break. A reggae groove eventually emerges; I like it. Hansford Rowe has a nice bass tone on this. The vocals return afterwards. The chorus has a catchy hook on the title phrase. The effects that they use are captivating. Cool track, with a potentially ear-worm chorus.Track 3 - Siren Song (5:07)The opening sound effects do indeed invoke the siren's song. The vocals enter and lead the instruments in with a slow groove. This one is a little bit "doom-y". I like the vocal sound with lots of reverb and echoes. The contrast between the heavy doom-laden verses and the somewhat lighter choruses is nice. Good track, very engaging.Track 4 - Pool of Mirrors (5:54)Electric piano with a vibrating tone starts this one out. This one is a little bit lighter at a moderate tempo. The music sort of floats. This is not too far removed from something that 21 Pilots might do (and I am very much on the record that I believe that 21 Pilots are a modern art-rock band). There is even something of a rap at around 3:30. The rhythm section drops out around 4:30 and there is a quieter section. Eventually, the instruments drop off one by one, leaving the main keyboard riff and an acoustic guitar lead. The bass takes over from the guitar, then some wordless vocals bring the song to a close.Track 5 - Heaven's Rain (7:18)This one starts gently with sustained keyboard sounds, electric piano and acoustic guitar. Big tom-tom sounds punctuate the sound before and during the vocals. The "enigmatic voice" is very much in use here. There are some BIG accents just prior to the 2:30 mark. A cool groove keeps the track moving. I like the bass lines on this album. In fact, after 4:30, the bass is featured. I like this instrumental section. It is symphonic much like early King Crimson on "Epitaph". I believe I hear a mellotron. I truly appreciate the fact that even though this is an electronic music project by nature, there are still great dynamic shifts and some real guitars and basses in use. It brings in the human factor. Good track. Track 6 - Screaming Sound Machines (4:57)This begins with an orchestral fade in, then a beat emerges. This has a great groove. The lead vocals are in a low register. I like the feel of this one. At 2:25, there is a bit of a "breakdown" segment with a cool analog synth tone. There is a nice, but brief, guitar solo at around 3:30, presumably from Steve Bonino. This is a pretty cool track. I like the false ending before the final chord.Track 7 - Heavy Water (7:34)A quiet riff over a synth bed starts things off here. Some dissonant piano and sound effects join in. This one is feeling like a slow burn. More sounds enter as we go along. At around the 2-minute mark, the rhythm section makes a beat, and the vocals are downright creepy sounding. I like the refrain of the title with the lead vocals singing other words. Things get quiet for a moment in the middle of the song. The music gets big and powerful at around the 5-minute point. While the drum programming isn't bad, I'd love to hear this with a live drummer, as it's a little stiff sounding sometimes. The rest of the sounds are much more fluid (no pun intended). Track 8 - Inviolate Fields (9:51)The electric piano is the primary sound initially, but the soundscape grows. Guest vocalist Laura Piazzai's voice adds a new dimension to the sound. I already am familiar with her from her work on the Massimo Pieretti album I have reviewed on this blog (see the labels menu); she's wonderful. There is an awesome fretless bass feature at around the 3-minute mark. Quinn Blanchard's violin is kind of spooky in the way that Jimmy Page's bowed guitar is on Led Zeppelin's "In the Evening"; cool! There is a vibraphone tone that is sort of dominating the sound at around 5 minutes, that buries Laura's vocals in the mix, I wish she was brought out more. She comes out more as the song progresses. The overall feel is pretty laid-back on this longest track. I like the triangles or whatever the percussion sounds they are using are at around 8:30. The track just sort of winds down at the end. Piazzai's voice is the stand-out feature of this track. Track 9 - Are Friends Electric? (5:17)This is a cover of a Gary Numan song. A cool bass riff is the motif on this one. This one is moderately fast. The vocal melody is kind of catchy. There is a low-register spoken word section in the middle with a cool rhythmic backdrop. This one has a bit of an 80s new-wave vibe. There is another spoken-word section with about one minute remaining. They ride the riff out to the song's conclusion. OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:Electronic music isn't my biggest area of expertise, but I generally liked this album. The biggest drawback is the drum machine in my opinion. Hansford Rowe's bass playing is so strong and provides a real human element to the sound, but sometimes the drum machine fills were so stiff and mechanical that they didn't quite mesh. I understand that they are coming from a point of view of being "sound machines", so maybe that is what they are going for. From my perspective, however, adding a live drummer would improve their overall sound and be less distracting than the stiff drum machine is to me. There was a lot that I DO like about this album. There are some great riffs and soundscapes and musical concepts here. The vocal sounds, even the processed ones, are very engaging and interesting. Rowe's bass work is a real standout for me. Alain Bellaiche seems to be a good guitarist when he gets the spotlight. This album is really about the electronic sounds that the founding pair of Jeremie Arrobas and Thomas Szirmay bring to the table, however, and in that aspect, they have succeeded. The guest musicians, particularly Steve Bonino, Laura Piazzai, and Quinn Blanchard add a lot to the album. I'll give this an overall score of 4 out of 5 stars (80%), but fans of electronic music stylings will probably like it even more.

items.body: Enter Mephistopheles Overcome by innocence and purity On a hell-bent path led to corrupt To destroy us all and rise above Goth music has always been hospitable to transformation: flesh into apparition, desire into doctrine, the nightclub into a temporary chapel. Pittsburgh industrial project ShadowMouth and Cleveland vocal trio The Elder Goths take that appetite for metamorphosis literally on The Promise of Alchemy/The Death of Chemistry, a paired single released August 12th and the final preview of ShadowMouth’s forthcoming debut album, Modern Alchemy. ShadowMouth is the project of multi-instrumentalist and songwriter Rick Polo, of Baroque Monody and Heck Vektor, with producer and drummer Brooks Farris of Electric Fox Studios. After the 2024 EP Purification By Fire and singles including Your Words, Not Mine and DOOM SCROLLERS vs HOLY ROLLERS, Polo reached outside his immediate circle for these two pieces, contacting The Elder Goths: Cassandra Bishop, Laura O’Janpa, and Gina Schultz, without having met them. “These songs were the result of me taking a shot in the dark and reaching out The Elder Goths group, who I had never met before, and asked if they would provide some of the striking beautifully haunting harmonies that are immediately apparent when first hearing their work,” says Polo. “But it turned out to be so much more than I could have imagined. The end result was an intense and and really heartfelt delivery which absolutely blew me away. This collaboration felt too important not to highlight. So we decided to release this a single ahead of the record.” That gamble pays off immediately on The Promise of Alchemy. Aphex Twin-like electronics move beneath spare guitar passages while Bishop’s lyrics describe awakening, perception, and the search for one’s place within a larger atmosphere. The Elder Goths bring an elegant, spectral grandeur that recalls Strange Boutique, Faith and the Muse, and the ceremonial scale of Dead Can Dance. Their layered voices give Polo’s machinery a sense of upward motion, turning alchemy into a metaphor for people entering the same space and becoming altered by the encounter. The Death of Chemistry, with lyrics by Schultz, pushes the collaboration toward darker territory. Its language circles blindness, consumption, manipulation, predation, and the dangerous seductions of appearances. Mephistopheles enters as an emblem of corruption, while bodily warnings – alarm, dread, instinctive recoil – suggest a consciousness struggling to recognize danger before persuasion overrides perception. The final image of being taken in by a “suntan and a grin” gives the song a wickedly contemporary sting: evil may arrive beautifully groomed, socially fluent, and camera-ready. Together, the songs form a compact study in attraction and corruption. One considers transformation as revelation; the other examines how easily perception can be bent by charisma, appetite, and spectacle. This tension gives the collaboration a compelling force, especially because the music itself began with an act of trust between strangers. Listen below and purchase the double single here. The Promise of Alchemy/The Death of Chemistry by ShadowMouth & The Elder Goths Formed in 2024 after its members crossed paths through Cleveland’s underground scene, The Elder Goths will perform at Pagan Pride Fest in Cleveland on August 15th. Their appearance on Modern Alchemy gives ShadowMouth’s coming album an intriguing final preview: four musicians meeting across projects and cities, testing what might happen when unfamiliar elements are placed in the same vesse Follow ShadowMouth: Instagram Facebook Bandcamp Follow The Elder Goths: Instagram Bandcamp The post ShadowMouth and The Elder Goths Collaborate on Twin Tracks “The Promise of Alchemy and The Death of Chemistry” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
