items.body: Based in Gothenburg, SYNVILLA treats music and moving images as organs within the same unruly body. Heavy experimental rock, psychedelia, post-punk, and noise meet video art that is seductive, threatening, and frequently difficult to separate from the performance itself. Riffs drag and buckle, rhythms take crooked routes, and warped melodies push through distortion with a streak of playful menace. During their live performances, SYNVILLA uses projected video as part of the stage presentation. While the band plays, footage of bodies and faces repeats, divides, and distorts across the screen, changing in step with the music. The projections give the audience a visual extension of the songs and place video art at the center of the concert experience. SYNVILLA return with their latest single, Milky Breath, released through Beans on Toast Records. The song accompanies the announcement of the forthcoming GRINDMOTHER EP. Thick drums give Milky Breath a heavy, deliberate gait. Psychedelic guitars slither around them in warped curves, while a buzzing low register carries the chest-deep vibration of a didgeridoo. Above this mass, the vocals quiver with witchy poise, stretching each phrase somewhere between a warning, an invitation, and an involuntary exhalation. The arrangement gains force through repetition as its parts return slightly damaged, bend out of shape, and eventually break into a physical act of release. SYNVILLA describes the song as a surrender of conscious control, with social masks falling away as bodily impulse assumes command. The title intensifies that tension: milk suggests nourishment and breath signals life, yet the two words together feel thick, close, and almost claustrophobic. Resistance registers as muscle memory, the body shaking loose the instructions it has learned to obey. Few smiles in recent memory have looked as hungry as the one occupying the Milky Breath video. A black-clad figure appears beneath two enormous horn-like forms while its mouth stretches into a crowded, impossible crescent, recalling the Mouth of Sauron in Peter Jackson’s The Return of the King. The eyes vanish, the head divides, and the grin remains fixed, as though it has taken possession of the person wearing it. Victor Cornelius turns that premise into five and a half minutes of analog-video mutation. Solarized pinks, acidic orange, and cyan pass over faces and anatomical forms. The central figure is duplicated into contact sheets, folded into bilateral symmetry, pressed behind mesh, and expanded into a featureless white oval. Banks of lidless eyes crowd the frame while faces swim beneath watery tracking errors, hands skitter across a doubled torso, and human figures collapse into stark silhouettes. Throughout these transformations, the enormous grin functions as a gruesome visual refrain. It survives every attempt to erase the face around it, repeatedly returning with its wet rows of teeth intact. By the final passage, the video resembles a late-night television transmission seized by an intelligence that has only recently learned the mechanics of a human smile. The collective has shared stages with Hällas, Skraeckoedlan, and MaidaVale, while appearing at festivals including Fuzztival, Muskelrock, and Sonic Ritual. items.body: REWORK have been around long enough to know that club music’s supposedly clean breaks with the past are usually rather messier affairs. Michael Kübler and Daniel Varga formed the Stuttgart electronic project in 2000 with French vocalist Laetitia Rometsch, releasing their first EP, Anyway I Know You, through Frankfurt’s Playhouse Records. Their 2003 debut album, Fall Right Now, brought together early cuts, including “You’re So Just Just,” and established the combination they would come to describe as “new wave house”: spare machines, clipped funk, European pop instincts, and vocals that regard seduction as a form of mild antagonism. Later records for Playhouse, Visionquest, Get Physical, and their own Exlove imprint continued to complicate the boundaries between house, techno, electro, and pop at a time when those distinctions still carried considerable tribal weight. Released through Exlove Records on July 17th, the three-track Disco Love Remixes EP returns to the title track of REWORK’s March 2025 release. The original followed 2024’s Never Again and a Get Physical release that paired REWORK’s updated version of “You’re So Just Just” with separate remixes by Cinthie and Seth Troxler with Ryan Crosson. The new collection brings together interpretations by Neu-Romancer and Jennifer Touch alongside REWORK’s own “Disco Love2,” a special edit that reaches back toward the economical architecture of their Playhouse years. Sira Kübler’s vocal gives “Disco Love” its human temperature, sitting against bass and percussion disciplined enough to make each small adjustment feel consequential. The Playhouse influence is explicit in “Disco Love2,” although the track avoids becoming an exercise in period reconstruction. Its disco vocabulary has been pared down until glamour becomes something harder, stranger and slightly severe. Neu-Romancer is the solo project of Laura Bailey, an Australian musician, producer and DJ originally from Fremantle and now based in Berlin. Her 2023 debut EP, Neue Romantika, appeared on Zanias’ Fleisch Records, drawing on Italo disco, darkwave, EBM, and New Romantic references across four original tracks and a Zanias remix. The record included “Remnants,” a collaboration with Kris Baha, while Bailey’s broader history includes playing bass with goth outfit VV & The Void and punk band CIERN, as well as performing in Zanias’ live group. Her connection with REWORK predates the present remix: the artists released the two-track Call You Up EP together in June 2025. For “Disco Love,” Neu-Romancer takes the material into a more insistent space. Her remix thickens the rhythmic motion and introduces a bouncing, almost predatory momentum, making the track feel as if it were designed for the point in a club night when conversation has ceased to be useful. Details accumulate without clutter, and the arrangement maintains a peculiar forward pressure even as its gestures become more expansive. Neu-Romancer Jennifer Touch is a Berlin-based producer, singer, live musician and DJ whose work draws in part on her upbringing in eastern Germany. After issuing her first solo record in 2014, she developed a body of work that moves freely between post-punk, industrial electronics, wave music and club production. Her albums Behind the Wall and Midnight Proposals appeared through FatCat Records in 2020 and 2023, respectively, followed by Aging at Airports through Fabrika Records in September 2025. She has also released music through Riotvan, Eskimo Recordings, and Live at Robert Johnson, and has collaborated with Curses and Paranoid London. Touch approaches “Disco Love” from another angle, bringing greater emotional abrasion to its polished frame. Her version pairs cold-wave textures with a forceful club structure, allowing tension to build around Sira Kübler’s vocals and the regimented percussion. The bass bears down with greater weight while the upper register remains brittle and exposed. It is an effective reminder of how closely post-punk’s severity and dance music’s physicality have always sat beside one another. Jennifer Touch That relationship between post-punk and dance music also explains the logic behind Exlove Records, REWORK’s own imprint. Its catalog moves between synthpop, house, techno, electro, post-punk and synthwave without treating genre boundaries as border control, with releases from REWORK alongside She Lies, Philipp Roller, Sugartin and A Youth. Across more than two decades, REWORK’s tracks have also been handed to Andrew Weatherall, Roman Flügel, Trentemøller, Magda, Paranoid London, Cinthie and Seth Troxler for reinterpretation. They have little need to prove their underground credentials. “Disco Love” sounds more interested in what can still be done with them. Listen to Disco Love Remixes below and order the EP here. items.body: Summer songs traditionally have an unfair advantage. They get cars with the windows down, imprudent decisions, swimming pools, romances improved by temporary geography. Soft Vein’s new single Another Summer seems suspicious of all that. Justin Chamberlain approaches the season as someone might regard an old photograph found in a drawer: with affection, perhaps, but also with the knowledge that whatever happened there has already escaped its participants. The title suggests recurrence, but Chamberlain sounds interested in what recurrence fails to restore. Another season comes around. The people inhabiting it have changed. The song, the final single from Soft Vein’s forthcoming All We’ve Known of Heaven, has some of the suave composure of Robert Palmer and the eccentric pop intelligence of John Foxx and Peter Gabriel. A rounded bass line moves beneath clipped vocal phrases and lush synthesizers, which periodically rise around Chamberlain without swallowing him. The staccato chant and hook are especially good, giving an otherwise sumptuous ballad a curious nervousness, as though somebody has prepared the perfect sentence and then discovered that speaking it aloud changes its meaning. This year, Soft Vein has moved further toward synthpop, although Chamberlain retains a detached, cerebral chill. Another Summer may be the most persuasive argument yet for that development: a beautiful arrangement can make emotional confusion more acute. The bass has an almost tactile roundness; the keyboards occasionally widen into luminous sheets; his voice stays exposed in the middle, stylish without becoming mannered. Every element appears to know exactly how much room it should occupy. Chamberlain sings softly, often close enough to conversational volume that his restraint becomes part of the song’s psychology. Soft Vein has always been interested in the humiliations of wanting something from another person: reassurance, sex, permanence, an explanation. Another Summer finds him contemplating communication; his delivery has the attractive uncertainty of a person willing to disclose something before deciding whether disclosure was wise. That divided temperament has followed Soft Vein from 2023’s Pressed in Glass through Through Blinds, the 2024 record that brought Chamberlain’s songwriting into sharper focus. The 2025 EP From Another Room, featuring remixes by Twin Tribes and Qual alongside covers of formative artists, offered a useful bridge. All We’ve Known of Heaven is now available for preorder ahead of its release through Artoffact Records. Soft Vein will mark the album with a September 11 Los Angeles release show at Zebulon, presented by Minty Boi, with Catherine Moan as direct support and Secret Attraction opening. Buy tickets here. items.body: Across the vast American sprawl, post-punk and darkwave have taken root in cities throughout the country, with each local scene giving the music its own character. Among the rising bands within that wider movement, Casket Cassette and Stare Away represent two distant geographic poles: Los Angeles and New York City, the City of Angels and Gotham, relentless sunshine and after-dark intensity. This summer, the bands have closed nearly 3,000 miles of continental distance on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour, the Los Angeles project’s first headlining run. Constant Laval Williams and Ben Nelson first became friends when Stare Away joined a Casket Cassette bill at Sip Studios in Jersey City, where they discovered common ground in Joy Division’s rhythmic force and Ian Curtis’s songwriting, as well as recovery, poetry, and the desire to exorcise personal damage through catharsis of a crowd. Both artists entered the tour with their most substantial releases to date. Casket Cassette’s third album, Reducer, released June 12, turns experiences of erasure, constriction, recovery, and the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires into a ten-song study of what survives when a life and community have been pared back. Post-Punk.com followed the record’s development through Kiss Me Awake and Show Me a Sign, songs that brought Williams’s doomed romanticism into sharper electronic relief. On July 31, Stare Away released its seven-song debut, In Absence, via à La Carte Records, drawing on Nelson’s seclusion after sobriety, the depths of addiction, and relationships that continued to exert their pull. Its closing track, Familiar, gave those concerns one of the album’s most immediate expressions. Onstage, their geographical and musical differences sharpen the pairing. Casket Cassette channels the strange darkness that flourishes beneath Los Angeles sunshine through electronic pressure and doomed pop melody, while Stare Away draws on Gotham’s nocturnal velocity with tensile bass, urgent guitar, and the close physical charge of an early post-punk club. As the tour enters its final stretch, Post-Punk.com spoke with Williams and Nelson about the records that guided Reducer and In Absence, the friendship behind the tour, the cultures of their respective cities, and the collaboration already waiting beyond the final date: Ben, in absence, feels like a reference to the terms “In Memoriam” or “To Absent Friends”. What kind of absence does the title refer to, and what emotional or thematic thread holds the album together? The record is a massive reflection on the past couple years of my life. I definitely secluded myself from a lot of aspects of living in New York City so I could just focus and make progress on better finding myself after getting sober. I just disappeared for a while from going out and was working full-time at a job I absolutely hated. I looked at myself & how insane the state of the world currently is, and put everything into my craft to reflect my own mysteries, questions & realizations of isolation, depths of addiction, and relationships I’ve had that were very important to me. I think when you put your heart into something physical and artistic, people will truly relate rather than follow like a cheap social media posting scheme and will feel much more fruitful and fulfilling in the end. I feel like I discovered more about myself throughout the process of writing this record than I ever would if I hadn’t. The title track sums up the entire record and each following track dissects it in its own way musically and lyrically. Sitting with Mike Morello in the studio and putting so much time and emotion into each song really tied it all up with a bow. Ben, which artists, records, or musical periods were foremost in your mind while making In Absence? Or writers and filmmakers perhaps? To really narrow it down, New Order’s “Movement” demos and writing sessions, The Cure’s “Faith” home demos, and The Sound’s “Jeopardy” record are in my everyday rotation. When it came down to pure influence, I really wanted to write from a direction as a band involved in the first wave with a maturing mid-80s attitude. The sculpting behind what defined an emerging underground genre is what I’ll always strive for when writing. Experimental films and beatnik writers of the late 50s and 60s called me to think more of vulnerability in expression when it came down to writing the lyrics. Ben, was there one song that unlocked the direction of In Absence and helped you understand what the rest of the record needed to become? “I Can’t Escape Myself” by the Sound. Truly a masterpiece of a track in my opinion. The daily hysteria of living life on life’s terms regardless of situation or control over one’s ability to have an answer for everything that shapes our identities and emotions is kind of a beauty in a sense, which makes us all unique in our own ways. The album art shot by Julie Lodhy really captured that reflection literally. Constant, what first set Reducer in motion, and how did the album develop from that initial idea into the finished record? I’d been spending most of my time focusing on crafting standout singles (Bouquet, Broken Tomorrow, etc.), and I wanted to return to another cohesive project. Specifically, for album #3, I wanted to respond to the erasure, reduction, and alienation I’d been feeling after returning home to LA from graduate school at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, and in the wake of the LA fires. In a short period of time, my community of friends and my childhood home had both burned, shrunk, or vanished. It was a period of interpersonal, mental, and physical loss. I first explored these themes in the context of inward reflection, and then expanded into an examination of my past and my relationship to others. I also chose to incorporate increasingly poetic elements (such as references to Robert Lowell’s Skunk Hour in Kiss Me Awake, a poem in the interlude, and various lyrics that leaned more deeply into nuanced metaphor). The instruments ended up expressing rage, loss, and existential claustrophobia via the use of heavy basslines and aggressive drums, coupled with ethereal anthemic synths and the occasional heartfelt guitar line. What made me fall in love with the darkwave and post-punk genres to begin with was their ability to honestly express pain and darkness while also transfiguring that same pain into something beautiful and danceable. I can only hope this new album achieved that same duality. Constant, the word “reducer” suggests compression, subtraction, or stripping something to its essential form. What does the title mean to you, and how does it relate to the album’s songs? I think that you summed it up nicely. Like the choke-chain collar in the cover art, the title reflects a feeling of constriction (a minimization of self, community and environment). If you have the kind of brain that I have, life can sometimes feel like a series of “reductions” almost like pruning a bonsai tree to try to stay “right sized.” This has always been the case for me (especially as someone in recovery), but to have those reductions unwillingly extend into the world around me was intense. I think the songs all mirror this differently. I tried to let them be eclectic; sometimes disparate elements in conversation with one another are more comprehensive than similar elements. On songs like Kiss Me Awake and Melting Angels, there’s a wide-open purgatorial feeling that’s at odds with poignant, pared-down lyrics. A song like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) is a bittersweet memory, a bleeding echo of a whole. Show Me a Sign and Becoming burst past constriction into raw expressions of existential energy (etc.). Harmoniously, the album was mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios, who works almost exclusively with analog equipment. The process of mixing with analog machines is also a reduction of the nebulous revisions and additions of modern DAWs; when effects were baked into the stems, they were made singular and permanent. The same is true for Matia’s raw, minimalistic approach to tracking vocals on songs I recorded in-studio such as Becoming. The stems of some songs like Elegy were compressed together onto tape, and then re-digitized. Constant, which artists and records exerted the strongest influence on Reducer, and where can you hear those influences entering the album? There is always a plethora of artists within (and outside of) the genre influencing me. These, of course, include the giants whose footsteps we walk in (ie. Joy Division, The Cure, Bauhaus, Siouxsie, etc.) as well as the peers I have walking beside me (check out my Spotify playlist for reference). If I had to narrow it down for this specific album, I’d say: Charlotte Sometimes by The Cure, But Not Tonight by Depeche Mode (specifically the intro), the body of work by Sad Madona (who I’ve done two collaborations with (including on Reducer), and who I’ve been hanging out with when I visit the EU), the music of my buddy Jamison (aka Gossip Cult), indie and indie-adjacent bands I used to listen to when I was a kid (like Beach Fossils, Surf Curse, The Drums, etc,), The Smiths, Atmosphere by Joy Division, Crystal Castles, experimental acid/trance/house music I used to dance to at illegal warehouse raves downtown, Nitzer Ebb, Pagliacci by Leoncavallo, and various movie soundtracks. As a result, songs like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) blend post-punk and indie/alternative, while songs like Show Me a Sign or Apathy are darkwave with elements of electronica and EBM. All of these influences have allowed me to move in a new direction while staying true to my voice. Constant, you are also a poet, photographer, and filmmaker. How did those other disciplines shape the lyrics, imagery, or structure of Reducer? For me, all these disciplines come from the same source but are expressed in different ways, each appropriate for different moments/needs. They all allow us as human beings to try to source meaning from existence and our universe; a meaning we will never fully reach, but a beautiful process regardless. Photography and film rely on choice of subject and composition to craft visual narrative or provoke thought, while music relies on a similar, auditory gut-instinct. These instincts are also involved in poetry, but the act of writing and editing a poem requires a more microscopic cartography; everything must belong, every word must connect, every image must work against or for the conceit of the poem. Poetry is my first love. I’m obsessed with it. There’s a beautiful anarchy to it, yet an intentionality that I don’t find to be fully true in music or photography. Sometimes my lyrics are hyper poetic, and sometimes I want a break from the intense scrutiny required of poetry. Sometimes I just want to write an immediately understandable or quasi-cliché lyric for the catharsis of that immediacy; just want to say “I love you” or “I miss you” and not “your shadow lingers in the wake of my delinquent dreams.” Coming out of the Writers’ Workshop and being in the process of finishing my debut collection of poetry, poetry played a much larger role in this album than in the past. As I previously mentioned, there is a full poem in the Interlude; songs like Elegy and Kiss Me Awake both use rhyme schemes (or non-rhyming free-verse) in their lyrics and poetic imagery that is a new frontier for the fusion of poetry and music for me. I have a very vivid imagination; it can be very cinematic at times. I daydream a lot. When I was writing Reducer, photography and cinematography also informed the songs for sure—if I can’t imagine a visual narrative in my head while listening back to a song, then it’s probably not a good song. Structurally, I always want my albums to have a narrative arc as well. In the case of Reducer, I wanted to start with a feeling of stasis and constriction that then erupted into defiant forward movement. Constant and Ben, how did the two of you first meet, and what were your initial impressions of one another, both personally and as musicians? Ben: We met at the Jersey City date of his first US tour with Blood Club and dustbowlchampion at Sip Studios, it was so cool to be able to meet from being on complete opposite sides of the country, everyone was so inviting and kind and it was awesome being able to appreciate each others music. It was like going to a new school and kicking it off with another kid in class with similar interests. Constant: Ben and I met a few years ago on my first-ever national tour with Blood Club and Dustbowlchampion. I had already been aware of Ben’s music after finding it online and would religiously listen to “My Cathedral” and “Something Strange” in my car on the way to work, so I was psyched when Ben was booked to play with all of us in Jersey City. I think we hit it off immediately; I could tell Ben just got it, it being the reason we all do what we do as artists. It’s really cool when you meet someone and are on the same wavelength. Stare Away. Photo by Constant Williams Constant and Ben, did you initially connect through any shared bands, records, or influences, and what helped that first connection develop? Ben: Definitely comparing our distinguished sounds to similar bands we both enjoy, I think Joy Division would be a top example because we both love Ian Curtis’ writing from a poetic standpoint, we did hit the exhibit in New York City together which was an awesome experience. I always learn of new books and readings to pick up from him. I also think it’s because I am a bassist and he came from a background of being a drummer, so I think a lot of bands that have that heavy foundation of rhythm sections drove a lot of our similar musical interests. Constant: For sure, I think most people who make music similar to us can connect over a shared love of many of the same bands (like the ones I mentioned before). I think it also helped that we both come to music at a poetic and existential angle, and we both could relate in terms of recovery from substances and the perspective shift that is required. Constant and Ben, what first made you want to collaborate musically, and when did the idea of touring together enter the conversation? We haven’t collaborated yet but we definitely have a song in the works. I think every time we’ve seen each other, we’ve thrown around the idea of touring together because we love each other’s music, and it especially made sense now that both of us are with BLCKJEANS. Ben, what appeals to you most about Reducer, and which song from the record do you find yourself returning to most often? I think Constants approach on the arrangements were genius. The drum breaks feel lyrical, the combination of synth selections and vocal melodies reached a part of this genre that hasn’t been touched upon yet, and classic Casket Cassette elements cultivated into his best work. My favorite part of all this is watching and listening as an artist grows musically. It’s hard to put my finger on a single song because each song has its own unique skeleton, but I have to go with “Apathy” as the track that’s always running through my head on this record. Constant, what do you enjoy most about In Absence, and which song on the album has become your personal favorite? Beyond how catchy and danceable its songs are, I love how authentic and genuine the album is. I also really enjoy the combination of quintessential 80’s New Wave sounds with dark Post-Punk melodies. The title track and Faithless Hum are my top favorites. Constant and Ben, your music shares certain post-punk and darkwave foundations while retaining two distinct identities. What do you think makes the bands complement each other so well on the same bill? Ben: I think our high-energy performances are what make this tour so special; the riffs throughout the night keep the atmosphere intense with movement and bring a great amount of nostalgia you feel at a goth club or punk show that you can’t capture at other shows. Our deep connection with the fans is what’s most important to me, hearing how the music can move through the audience and watching kids get lost in their dancing with their eyes closed while we’re playing on stage is so cool being able to resonate that from the stage. Constant: I think we complement each other because we both bring a similar energetic performance style, matching high energy with a candid sincerity. Ben’s music leans more towards post-punk with moments of darkwave, while my music leans more towards darkwave with moments of post-punk. I think that also creates a “yin and yang” effect for our live shows; two sides of the same coin. Casket Cassette. Photo by Aaron Jay Young Constant, you come from Los Angeles, while Ben is based in New York City. How have the music scenes and cultures of those cities shaped your respective projects, and what similarities do you recognize between them? And what do you think is different? Ben: I think New York City’s music scene is so diverse, which makes it such a beautiful and thriving location for musicians and showgoers. You can hit a punk show, an electronic show, hardcore show, or jazz club in the same borough in the same night. It’s wicked, I love it. I think LA is quite the same besides the traffic haha, but I think the diversity of people and genres is the best and most important similarity of both cities, keeping live music thriving. New York City in general has a million places to find and take inspiration from. Taking late night subway rides can create a huge narrative story in its own way, walking in the parks and seeing all different types of fashion and taking everyone’s unique sense of expression and sensing love and unfortunate disparities throughout the air can present all kinds of thoughts and ideas to put down on paper, it becomes its own dimension and reality that spews inspiration for lyrics and especially beat and rhythm. The nightlife through dive bars and street festivities is an overwhelming resource of artistic relation. You can simply sit in a moment, look around, and take in so much that you can’t find anywhere else. I try to take the mood and energy of wherever I was that night or night before to the writing process to resemble the city’s grit and hardstyle energy that keeps it alive. Constant: I think growing up in Los Angeles has informed my music a lot. There’s a strange duality to the shiny movie stars, warm beaches, and perpetual sunshine that is surrounded by industrial decay, violence, and broken dreams. I think my music has a similar duality, being both deeply sad and deeply danceable. That’s a strange combo that (I hope) works. It definitely reflects how I grew up and who I am; I never truly fit into any one box. On the contrary, despite being visually more gothic and less “shiny” than LA, I feel as though the scene might be a bit less substantial in size in New York City, but I only know a little from my limited experience. It has always made me laugh that the places with the most goths are often the ones that punish us with bright sunlight (ie. Los Angeles, Mexico City, San Antonio, etc., with the exception of Chicago). I love New York, and I do think there is a kinship between the two cities, and certainly they are two of the most important musical hubs in the world. Constant and Ben, what are you each most excited about on this run, and what kind of experience do you hope audiences take away from seeing both projects in the same room? Ben: I’m really stoked to finally play these new songs live and also give the fans a chance to sing the songs that got us here with us. My absolute favorite part is inspiring younger showgoers to keep pushing their craft; the young musicians are the main reason I do this 100%. I started going to shows around 12-13 years old at VFWs and want to relive how I felt when people rushed to the stage to snag the mic from the vocalist to scream the lyrics. We want to go against the grain as much as possible so we get sweaty with everyone on stage with us during ‘Parting Ways’. It just started out of a last-minute call-up on our first show in San Diego so I just wanted to try and accomplish that every single night regardless of the size of the audience. I was pretty nervous at first, but I know the fans have such a fun time being able to dance underneath the lights with us, and that’s what matters the most. I hope the audience can take away a fresh new ear for Post-Punk music and can feel like they’re at a Factory or CBGB show. I just want people to feel free in a safe space and take home an amazing show experience. Constant: I’m excited to play shows with Stare Away and all our awesome local openers because I know the audience is going to have a great experience! As my first headliner tour, I’m also really excited to get to play a longer set for fans; I’m always bummed when someone comes up to say hi and is sad that I didn’t play a specific song; hopefully having a fuller set mitigates some of that disappointment. Another favorite part of tour for me is meeting the amazing people who listen to my music; none of this would be possible without them, and they mean everything to me. All I want is for them to have a night where they can let go and enjoy themselves during these crazy times. Constant and Ben, once the tour is over and both albums have had time to settle into the world, what does each of you have planned for 2027, and do you envision further collaborations? Ben: As soon as we get back, I plan on just getting right back to constructing the direction of the next record. I want to find the perfect hybrid kit to add to our live shows and just make something different. I feel like a lot of bands just get trapped in the same sound, playing the same riffs. I definitely want to get my head into a new book and maybe pick up some weird new hobby, but I think I just want to challenge myself towards a new direction to take Stare Away. Constant: I recently won a literary award, and as a result I will be releasing a book of poetry in 2027 called Elegy with Beautiful Child, available for preorder from Milkweed Editions. My lifelong dream (even before music) has always been to publish a book of poetry, so this is a really important moment in my life! There is also a Stare Away x Casket Cassette song in the works, and Ben and I are good friends, so it’s definitely not the last you’ll be hearing from both of us.§ Casket Cassette’s Reducer is out now. Listen below, and Order Here. REDUCER by Casket Cassette Stare Away’s In Absence is out now. Listen below and Order Here. In Absence by Stare Away The end of the Reducer tour leaves both artists with fresh work already taking shape. Nelson plans to begin developing the next Stare Away record as soon as he returns to New York, introducing a hybrid drum kit while pushing the project toward unfamiliar methods. Williams will turn toward the January 2027 publication of Elegy with Beautiful Child, his debut poetry collection and winner of the 2025–26 Jake Adam York Prize. A Stare Away and Casket Cassette song is also underway, extending a friendship that began on a shared bill into the studio. The itinerary continues August 12 at Beat Kitchen in Chicago, followed by Minneapolis, Denver, Salt Lake City, Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco before their shared run closes August 22 at Summer Fox Brewing – Tower in Fresno. items.body: Horror Vacui Shadows Sanctuary Artoffact Records The layoff taken by Italian goth rock vets Horror Vacui since their last record has resulted in a new label and some line-up shuffling, but if you’ve tracked the path they’ve walked since their 2012 debut it won’t surprise you to learn that those aren’t the only things new to Shadows Sanctuary. A good ways removed from the crust influenced deathrock of In Darkness You Will Feel Alright, their fifth LP is a more integrated yet less showy affair than anything they’ve yet attempted. They might not be immediately apparent, but subtler moves like the harmonic colour on the chorus of opener “Dispossed” playing off the tight but sparse post-punk rhythm of the verse are more reflective of Shadows‘ priorities, and indeed, the slow winnowing away of the band’s punk roots and the uptick in more spidery and moody pure goth rock feels like it’s finally reached its apotheosis with this record. Oddly, that shift doesn’t yield more of the ascendant anthems (a la “Consolation Prize”) or compositional experiments (“Unreachable”) that the preceding LP Living For Nothing hinted at as their future. Instead, it’s more measured and reflective fare, like the lilting roll of “Eventide”, which is representative of Shadows Sanctuary. Even in the LP’s most raucous moments, like the scaling leads of “A Sunny Day” which slide overtop a dead simple thumping beat, the band sounds more akin to the theatrical excess of 90s acts like Corpus Delicti than any deathrock forbearer you’d care to name. Similarly, the instrumentation and arrangement of “Midnight” are simple enough, but it ends up having a plaintive if not downright romantic cast. “Skyless Eyes” is plenty propulsive, but the focus stays on atmosphere rather than aggression. It’s tempting to speculate as to the reasons behind this shift in Horror Vacui’s sound during their break – previous guitarist Marzia shifting to the drumkit, the arrival of new guitarist Vasu, the pandemic, the irresistible drift towards “mature” records – but again, a general sense of drift between dark rock subgenres has been part and parcel of the band for a while. They’ve long used the motto “punker than dark, darker than punk” to express this ambiguity, and while it still holds in theory on Shadows Sanctuary, the record does find one half of that dichotomy eclipsing the other. Buy it. Shadows Sanctuary by Horror Vacui The post Horror Vacui, “Shadows Sanctuary” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Welp. Better late than never. It's Kvlt Kolvmn's a-bit-more-than-halfway through 2026 best of list! Strap into your frostiest pair of dungaroos. It's gonna get wild.Black metal has had a very curious year for me. While I would say about half of the records I've listened to in the genre have felt like all-time bangers, the other half have put me to sleep. So in honor of that, I'll be presenting half a top 10 list. You're welcome. More awesome, however, is Boeli's incredible top 10, which features a handful of records I had yet to hear prior to reading his selections. Let's just say that good taste abounds as his list unfolds.But no more delay. Here are our iciest picks of 2026 so far.Stay frosty.-Jonathan AdamsTop Albums of 2026 So FarJonathan’s ListSaidan - Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s WristAs made plain when I waxed ineloquent a few weeks ago regarding the benefits of embracing the cringe in your life, I’m a BIG fan of Saidan. I would contend that their four album run thus far is one of the most consistently impressive in recent black metal, with each record refining and tactfully building upon what came before. Given this dynamic, it should come as no surprise that Fangdriller: Scars Beneath Memory’s Wrist is not only the band’s most complete and fantastic album thus far, but also the best extreme music record of the year so far. For me, it’s not close. What Saidan manages to channel here is a superb blend of melodic black metal, punk aesthetics, and power metal speed (replete with memorable hooks, punchy breakdowns, and manically aggressive tremolo shred sessions). It’s a relatively unique mixture that works due to genuinely gorgeous songwriting, which allows each sound to coexist seamlessly and interdependently without giving the listener genre-bending whiplash. The base is always black metal, and Saidan writes like a black metal band expanding the margins of the genre’s template with tasteful aggression. But their inclusion of other styles only works to sharpen and deepen listeners’ immersion in the world they’re creating. There isn’t a dull moment on this thing, and I frequently find myself hitting play again immediately after “Memory” fades into static. It’s addictive as hell. And, ultimately, that’s what I want from a record. I want to be transported, invited into a sonic world that’s cohesive enough to keep my undivided attention, and varied enough to never feel stale. And that’s exactly what Saidan provide with this absolute gem of a record. It’s my favorite thing I’ve heard so far this year, and I have a hard time imagining it being supplanted. Melodic black metal perfection.  FANGDRILLER: Scars Beneath Memory's Wrist by Saidan Miserere Luminis - SideraSpeaking of immersion, few albums so far this year have gripped me to the degree that Sidera, the third full-length from Montreal-based Miserere Luminis, has. Man oh man is this an exquisite slab of melody-heavy and deeply atmospheric black metal. The compositions are simply fantastic, winding and building into a delicious labyrinth of emotionally devastating delight. The musicianship on display here is also superb, allowing these tracks to breathe in the appropriate places before laying the black metal hammer down to glorious effect. It’s a fantastic showing from a band that has yet to release a dud, and I cannot wait to see where they transport us next.  Sidera by Miserere Luminis Worm - NecropalaceOne of the most hyped and ballyhooed records of the first half of 2026, I was honestly ready to judge this thing pretty harshly given initial impressions I’d heard from friends around the band's shift in tone. Happy to say I was dead wrong, as Necropalace feels like the most natural direction in the world for Worm to go after spending significant time with it. In a similar vein to Fangdriller, this record is just FUN. The songwriting is gothic and propulsive, creating an almost theatrical atmosphere that’s deeply enjoyable to sit in. One would never have guessed at Worm’s doomy roots by hearing Necropalace, thus is its genuine quality as a black metal album. Can’t recommend it highly enough, and plan on giving this thing many more spins throughout the year.  Necropalace (24-bit HD audio) by Worm Ultha - A Light So DimUltha is one of the most unpredictable and strangely amazing collectives working in the black metal sphere today, and A Light So Dim is unequivocally their boldest experiment to date. Thankfully, it works on almost every level. While the tonal shifts may look jarring on paper, Ultha’s unique skill of pulling various sound tapestries and weaving them into a robust whole is on full display here, and there isn’t a thing I’d change about this record. It is a long journey, which may be off-putting to some. But rest assured the time will be well spent. This is my favorite of the group’s records so far and a musical odyssey well worth taking. Genuinely brilliant stuff from these German geniuses.  A Light So Dim by ULTHA Misotheist - De PinteWell, enough pansy ass beautiful/experimental poser black metal, amirite?? JK naturally. While I’m a huge fan of bands that push the black metal formula to the fringes of trve, I’m still a devotee of the core sonic nastiness that made this genre the pariah it is in the music world. Enter Misotheist and their brilliant fourth full-length outing De Pinte. Like your black metal with a hefty dose of buzzsaw dissonance and tremolo violence? You’re in luck! This record absolutely slays. The first three tracks in particular are nothing short of a masterclass in black metal done right, with enough audio violence to sate even the thirstiest fan. But it’s the records fourth cut that shows the band’s capabilities most notably, presenting a doomier side that slows down the tempo but never once minimizes the menace or aggression these enigmatic Norwegians are known for. It’s a brilliant album that has received many a spin from yours truly and a true highlight of 2026.  De Pinte by Misotheist Boeli’s Kvlt kolvmn Top 10: Where Kvltvre Goes to Feed the Vvltvres10. Einherjer - LifebloodBy virtue of another folk-tinged black metal indebted band not making the cut for reasons of probable sketch, Einherjer just made my top 10 spot even though it’s hardly been out long enough to form a proper opinion.One thing I can say without hesitation, is that I quite enjoy the Norwegian Viking metallers trajectory since I last actively listened to them about a decade ago. While Av Oss, For Oss was an occasionally engaging if fairly monotone exercise in mid-paced black metal, Lifeblood is a much more colorful and generally more dynamic and melodic affair, and while still rooted in black metal, the branches of its world tree sapling have grown to embrace heavy metal and folk metal more and more. I appreciate their more melodic and varied approach, and would appreciate it even more with some more tempo variation and a bit of judicious editing. That being said, there are times I long for this subgenre like no other, and this year Einherjer have been its prime deliverer so far.  Lifeblood by Einherjer 9. Burnt Lodge / Veytik - Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split)Another somewhat late entry, I had almost completely missed this release, and was well and truly excited when I saw Burnt Lodge had new stuff out. Their 2024 release Intergenerational Anamnesis is one of my favourite iterations of Native American Black Metal. This particular micro-genre is a particular favorite of mine, and alongside Blackbraid and Nechochwen, Burnt Lodge sits among its top practitioners. Had this been a full album,. And had I discovered it earlier, this one might have sat quite a bit higher.While I also quite enjoy Veytik’s thrasher, Hellenic and Obsequiaesque escapades, they have not yet managed to grab me like Burnt Lodge does.  Anchors Plunged Off Helluland (Split) by Burnt Lodge 8. Pure Wrath - Bleak Days AheadI shall lazily refer you to my previous musings on Pure Wrath’s latest in Mays Kvlt Kolvmn.  Bleak Days Ahead by Pure Wrath 7. Stormkeep - The Nocturnes of IswylmOn their latest, bombasically titled album, Stormkeep took me by storm out of the gate, although I’m not yet wholly sure they’ll remain in my top 10 for the year entire. I generally like my black metal adorned with a serious amount of low-end, contrary to its traditional sound. While Stormkeep toe the line of what I enjoy production wise, the mix of spooky whimsy, expansive songwriting and exhilarating choruses managed to perk my ears up considerably. The gruff, charming and incredibly catchy gang shouts of opener “The Taste of Immortal Blood” are choice as hell, and while I could do with some more hooks like those to get my very mortal blood a-pumping in the mid section before the last two tracks offer a convincing coda, I suspect the album may need some more time to gestate before it truly settles in. The Nocturnes Of Iswylm by Stormkeep 6. Antrisch - Expedition III: RenitenzpfadAtmospheric black metal might be one of the most oversaturated and justly maligned sub-genres, but when done right, it can also be one of it’s most powerful. Of course your definition of “right” will vary, and there are many roads to Rome. Enter Antrisch, whose take on the sub-genre is one I would use as a prime example of doing atmoblack well. Antrisch unleash a vicious, razor-sharp blackened assault, while adorning their music with a powerful, iterative concept of (historical) exploration of some very inhospitable environments.While previous album Die Passage’s arctic voyage was an obvious fit for Antrisch’s icy timbre, Renitenzpfad might be equally if not more exciting for its less obvious theme of the hardships endured and horrors dished out by Spanish colonisers in the Americas. With all of Antrisch’s biting venom, this time empowered by topical and tasteful atmospheric interludes, sampling and thematic instrumentation, they once again succeed in telling a story and immersing their audience in it, without ever diluting their vicious, energetic core sound. Smart, urgent, dynamic and varied, while remaining remarkably cohesive;  Expedition III is another successful iteration in these Germans’ discography. EXPEDITION III : Renitenzpfad by Antrisch 5. Ashbringer - SubglacialI stand by my original review; anything close to 2019s Absolution would have topped any list, whether Black Metal specific or not. Time has both made me lost sight of Subglacial (who releases an album in January, I ask you!?), while also softening my initial dashed expectations for another long-form atmoblack magnum opus. My expectations should not make for a good or bad album in the end, and Ashbringer’s wintry yet somehow warm and nostalgic 2026 release is absolutely a good album. Go listen to it if you haven’t yet, and then go listen to Absolution.  Subglacial by Ashbringer 4. Apolaustic - No Plenitude Without SufferingWere it not for a scheduling snafu on my end, I would have reviewed this melodic black metal gem in April, and could now get away with another short referral to something I wrote before. Alas, no luck. I did not, and you shall now suffer my relative plenitude. I picked up the promo for this album based on a promising single at the time, and was further pleasantly surprised by an album that proved deep and expansive enough that I was still forming a full opinion by teh time the review deadline slipped through my powerless fingers. A couple months later, I can tell you with full confidence that this is my favourite “pure” melodic black metal album of the year so far, defining meloblack in the vein of something like Mare Cognitum or Houle. Decidedly less maritime (in title or sound) and with a much more space-faring vibe going on, Apolaustic’s ability to write dynamic songs with an undeniably kinetic mix of melody, technicality and songwriting chops should be no surprise to anyone who is familiar with project mastermind Romain Negro’s previous membership of excellent progressive/medloic/technical death metal band Stortregn.Indeed, comparing No Plenitude Without Suffering to Stortregn’s younger black metal sibling would not be entirely inappropriate, as it exhibits the same mix of soul, shred and sheer scope, if so far lacking absolute supernova’s like "Grand Nexion Abyss” or “Xeno Chaos”.For any enjoyers of melodic black metal of quality and pedigree unfuckwithable, look no further. But please do actually, there’s three more entries. No Plenitude Without Suffering by APOLAUSTIC 3. Hellripper - CoronachAs it stomps, gallops and jigs between fun, fury and a finisher of true grandeur, since I last covered it in April’s KK Helripper’s Coronach has proven both it’s endlessly engaging vibrancy, and its ability to engage so many of the things that can make a metal album great, but rarely show up on the same album. It’s fun, it’s solemn and majestic, it's catchy, it’s angry, it brims with energy and sounds like it’s about to rip out of its restraints, but never gets speed metal sloppy. Incredibly varied yet uniformly great, Coronach should show up in quite a few lists come year’s end, and not just the blackened ones.  Coronach (24-bit HD audio) by Hellripper 2. The Silver - Looking Glass Hymnal BlueI honestly have no idea if this is even black metal, which is also the only reason it’s not on number one. The Silver’s sophomore amalgamation of metal styles is the kind of breath-taking bricolage that makes me want to rip up my clothes and howl at the moon. Rooted in a deep romanticism, indulgent, baroque, gothic and maximalist yet never tasteless, this album embodies what I love in my heavy music while eschewing everything I don’t.Considering its members comprise veterans of Horrendous (recognize those eardrum-flayingly awesome shrieks yet?) and Crypt Sermon, the quality is perhaps not as surprising, but while neither of those other projects fully mesh with my preferences, this one really, really does.The only criticism I would level at it is that “Tow Candles” and “My Lone Dark Lantern” are simply so good that they threaten to cast shadows as dark as their lights are bright, and thus obscure their surrounding companions.  Looking Glass Hymnal Blue by The Silver 1. Miserere Luminis - SideraBut of course, my pride as a genre stickler could not survive placing anything at number oen that is not unequivocally BLACK METAL.Luckily, there is nothing disingenuous about this placement. Miserere Luminis, another stellar band out of Quebec (seriously, what’s the secret??) gracefully take the year’s twisted yet mesmerisingly beautiful throne. With an ear for blackened melodic rapture akin to Houle, riffs as snaky and entrancing as late-stage Ulcerate and the soul-rending cathartic qualities of Selbst,Sidera goes above and beyond its influences, featuring truly engrossing compositions replete with strings and probably my favorite drumming of the year so far. Gorgeous, sad and fragile without losing the razor-sharp bite that atmospheric black metal so often lacks, I have no doubt this tour-de-force will remain at or near the top come final list season, and stay in rotation far beyond the year’s end. Sidera by Miserere Luminis

items.body: Crucifera, the solo industrial project of New Jersey-based musician Danielle Astraea, released the single “Paint” on July 24, 2026. The track is self-released independently and available digitally on Bandcamp and other streaming platforms. It follows the debut album, “Exostential,” released April 3, 2026. “Paint” mixes industrial, trip-hop, gothic trap and witch-house elements. Astraea wrote, produced, recorded and mixed the track herself in her home studio, and Sebastian Komor (Icon of Coil, Xenomorph Productions) handled mastering, the same role he held on “Exostential.” The song is a dark, abrasive exploration of cognitive dissonance, attribution error and tribalistic projection, built around how people reduce other people to fixed caricatures – either idealized or demonized – rather than responding to who they actually are. Astraea describes her overall sound as “crunchy ethereal industrial music for spiders.” She works without a traditional drum kit, building the rhythm tracks from processed field and sound-design textures rather than sampled or programmed drum sounds, and composes each song first on acoustic piano and guitar before building out the electronic production in her home studio. Paint by crucifera About Crucifera Crucifera is the solo project of Danielle Astraea, a self-taught multi-instrumentalist, producer and visual artist based in New Jersey, United States. Astraea began her professional career in the arts and creative direction in 2000, but kept her original music private for years before releasing it under the Crucifera name. She writes, records, mixes and produces every Crucifera track herself, starting each composition on acoustic piano or nylon guitar before building the finished arrangement digitally in her home studio. Crucifera’s debut full-length album, “Exostential,” was released on April 3, 2026, preceded by the singles “saVior” and “Martyr Box.” The album was mastered by Sebastian Komor of Icon of Coil and Xenomorph Productions; “Martyr Box” was mixed by Steven Seibold of Hate Dept. Astraea has also contributed composition and remix work to other industrial acts outside her solo output. “Paint,” Crucifera’s first single since “Exostential,” continues the project’s fusion of acoustic songwriting roots and industrial electronic production, with Komor again handling mastering. A new Crucifera EP is planned for later in 2026, followed by a second full-length album in 2027.

items.body: Korean vocalist Hye-gang and Polish producer DustCats have released “Tired with all these, for restful death I cry”, a single continuous drone and ambient piece running just over 35 minutes, on the Wrocław netlabel Ubocze Rec. (catalog Ubocze Rec. 089). The digital release went up on Bandcamp on August 7, 2026, as a name-your-price download with a suggested price of 27 and a minimum of 10. The track’s title is drawn from the opening line of Shakespeare’s Sonnet 66. It builds from field recordings DustCats made in Bangkok, Thailand, layered with a generative drone assembled from six Thai-sourced samples controlled through sliders and macros in Ableton. Over that bed, Hye-gang reads a William Wordsworth poem and Sonnet 66 in a spoken-word style DustCats describes as “very ASMR.” The music was recorded in Wrocław, Poland, while the cover artwork and an accompanying video were shot in Jelenia Góra, Poland, using a microscope attachment on a phone camera. DustCats describes the piece’s assembly: “While in Thailand a while ago, I made a lot of field recordings, but after returning, I had no idea how to put them together. Meanwhile, Hye-gang, a friend from Korea with whom I’d already collaborated on Ashes and Kalpa, sent me her recordings, where she reads a Wordsworth poem and Shakespeare’s Sonnet 66. […] I also experimented with a generating drone that combined six different samples, which could be controlled using sliders and macros in Ableton. All the samples were Thai ones. All this, combined, resulted in a 35-minute suite recorded at once.” Tired with all these, for restful death I cry by Hye-gang \ DustCats About Hye-gang and DustCats DustCats is a Poland-based producer who builds drone and ambient pieces from field recordings, active on Ubocze Rec., the Wrocław netlabel run by Łukasz Bejnar and Kuba Knoll since 2019. Hye-gang is a South Korea-based vocalist and collaborator who contributes spoken-word readings to DustCats’ productions; by DustCats’ own account, the pair had previously worked together on releases titled “Ashes” and “Kalpa” before “Tired with all these, for restful death I cry.” Ubocze Rec. operates as a non-commercial netlabel associating solo acts and projects from across electronic and experimental music, with releases spanning industrial, field recordings, lo-fi, ambient, techno, electro and IDM. The label’s catalog is anchored by Łukasz Bejnar’s own recording alias Uchylak, whose 2025 album “Zimna Gmina” received prior Side-Line coverage; label artist Dariusz Jackowski’s EP “Bezimienny” was also covered by Side-Line following its August 2026 release. “Tired with all these, for restful death I cry,” released alongside two other Ubocze Rec. titles on August 7, 2026, extends that catalog into a two-person, cross-continental field-recording piece built from source material gathered in Thailand, Poland and South Korea.

items.body: From 12 August 2026, today that is, small European record labels and mail-order businesses selling CDs and vinyl across EU borders face a new layer of packaging bureaucracy. The environmental goal behind the PPWR is easy to understand, but the way cross-border EPR has been organised is much harder to defend. Actually, it’s not defendable at all, and you wonder how otherworldly these bureaucrats really are. A packaging law with consequences far beyond packaging Today, 12 August 2026, the EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, better known as PPWR, starts applying across the European Union. Most consumers will barely notice, but independent labels, artists, specialist record shops and small mail-order businesses could notice very quickly. The PPWR is meant to reduce packaging waste, improve recycling and make producers pay for the collection and treatment of packaging they place on the market. Few small businesses will object to that principle. The trouble however starts when a tiny seller ships directly to a customer in another member state. Under the new framework, the seller can become the packaging producer for EPR purposes in the country where the order is delivered and where the packaging will eventually become waste. A German label mailing a CD to France can therefore face French EPR obligations. A vinyl order sent to Germany brings German obligations into play. Austria, Italy, Finland or Portugal each add another national compliance system. The European Commission’s own 2026 guidance confirms that a webshop selling packaged goods directly to an end user in another member state is the producer for EPR purposes in that destination country. Who actually proposed this bureaucratic PPWR atrocity? The cross-border representative requirement was not an amendment dreamed up later by the European Parliament or quietly added during negotiations with national governments as it was already present in the European Commission’s original PPWR proposal of 30 November 2022. In that draft it appeared as Article 40(2). The Commission proposed that a producer should appoint an EPR representative in every member state other than its own where it placed packaging on the market. After the legislation was negotiated and renumbered, that provision became the current Article 45 requirement. So where did it come from? The author of the proposal was the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment, DG ENV. The proposal was then adopted by the first Commission headed by Ursula von der Leyen on 30 November 2022. The two politicians who publicly fronted the package that day were – of course who else – the climate extremists Frans Timmermans, then Executive Vice-President of the European Commission responsible for the European Green Deal, and Virginijus Sinkevičius, then European Commissioner for Environment, Oceans and Fisheries. Both presented and publicly proudly defended the Commission’s new packaging rules at their launch. Parliament had the chance to remove the PPWR, but did nothing But the responsibility does not end with the Commission. A Commission proposal does not become EU law on its own. In the European Parliament, the politician with primary responsibility for steering the PPWR through the legislature was Belgian MEP Frédérique Ries of Renew Europe/Mouvement Réformateur. She was appointed rapporteur for the Parliament’s Environment Committee in January 2023, drafted the parliamentary report and handled compromise amendments and negotiations on Parliament’s behalf. The parliament had ample opportunity to amend or remove it during the legislative process, but surprisingly they hardly tried so the requirement survived. On 24 April 2024, the European Parliament approved the PPWR by 476 votes in favour, 129 against and 24 abstentions. In short, a large majority of elected MEPs voted for the package that contained it. National governments signed off too On 16 December 2024, the Council formally adopted the PPWR. The vote was 26 countries in favour and one against. The only member state that voted against the final regulation was Slovakia. Belgium voted for it. France voted for it. Germany voted for it. The Netherlands voted for it. Italy, Spain, Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Poland and 16 other countries voted for it as well. There is no shortage of people or institutions to hold politically accountable. One small mailorder, but several national PPWR systems For the independent music business, the result is painfully concrete. A label may press 300 copies of an album and sell 150 at home. The remaining copies go to customers scattered across Europe: ten to France, six to Germany, three to Finland, two to Portugal, one to Slovenia. Those are ordinary cross-border sales in what is supposed to be a Single Market. For packaging compliance, however, they can become separate national obligations. There is no single EU packaging registration covering all 27 countries. There is no central declaration filed in Belgium, Germany or France that follows the seller across the Union. National registers, national schemes, national reporting and locally established representatives remain part of the system. That may be manageable for Amazon or Universal Music, but It is a very different proposition for a mailorder selling a few thousand records per year. Small volume does not mean no obligation Many independent sellers will logically assume there must be a threshold below which none of this matters. But, there is no broad exemption based on turnover or parcel numbers. The PPWR does provide lighter reporting for producers placing less than 10 tonnes of packaging per year on a national market. And almost every indie label or mailorder will sit far below that figure. The lighter reporting rules, however, do not erase the underlying producer status or the country-by-country EPR structure. A label may send only a few kilograms of cardboard into a country during an entire year and still face fixed administrative costs that bear little relation to the amount of waste it actually generates. A few records can trigger hundreds of euros in costs, per destination that is A 2026 price list published by EPR compliance provider Eldris illustrates how quickly those costs can rise. Its published packages range from roughly €360 per year for Germany to €1,485 for Slovenia, depending on the country and services included. Adding the listed prices for all 27 EU member states produces a total of around €17,860 for the first year. These are commercial prices, and other providers may charge less, but you get an idea how ridiculous this has gotten. Businesses can also handle parts of the administration themselves. Yet the reason such an EPR compliance industry exists is obvious: a small seller is being asked to cruise through different registers, schemes, representatives, declarations and deadlines across multiple countries. The economics turn ugly very fast. If a label sells 20 records into one country and spends €400 annually on compliance there, that fixed cost equals €20 per order. Sell five records and it becomes €80 per order, before postage, VAT, payment fees, manufacturing, packaging and artist royalties enter the calculation. Stopping sales to that country then becomes cheaper than complying with the rules required to sell there. And that is what is happening now. Small retailers have already started cutting EU destinations. German businesses Pikecraft and Valkyrie Parts explicitly blame PPWR for reducing the countries they will serve, while Betta Botanicals in the US has stopped EU shipping altogether. The Commission knew it had created a problem with the PPWR, but still went ahead This is where the story becomes particularly uncomfortable for the European Commission and all the politicians involved, hundreds that is in every member state. By the end of 2025, the Commission was already trying to suspend the very authorised-representative requirement that had appeared in its own 2022 proposal. It proposed delaying the obligation for EU businesses until 1 January 2035, explicitly recognising that fragmented EPR requirements create barriers to cross-border business inside the Single Market. That attempt failed to produce relief before 12 August 2026. On 24 June 2026, the Council reported that negotiations on the proposed changes had been discontinued after a large majority of member states raised strong reservations. The regulation therefore reached its general application date with the problem unresolved. The Single Market starts looking less single after PPWR This is the contradiction at the heart of the system. Europe spent decades removing barriers to cross-border trade, only to construct a packaging regime capable of making the destination country relevant again for a €20 CD. Charging a seller according to the amount of packaging waste it creates is defensible. Making that seller establish separate compliance arrangements because five people in another member state bought records is something else. As a result, large retailers will absorb the change while small sellers will reduce their reach significantly. PPWR does not discriminate between Amazon and an indie label on paper. That is precisely the problem. It subjects radically different businesses to fixed country-by-country obligations whose cost Amazon can spread over millions of parcels while an independent label may have only three customers in that country. Equal rules do not produce equal consequences when the compliance cost is largely fixed. It remains to be seen whether common sense will return to Brussels.

items.body: British electronic musician and producer William Orbit has died at the age of 69. His family confirmed he died at home on July 23, 2026. Orbit, born William Mark Wainwright on December 15, 1956, in Enfield, north London, is best known for producing Madonna’s 1998 album “Ray of Light” and for a series of remixes for artists across pop, rock and electronic music during the 1990s. Orbit’s family announced his death in a statement posted on social media: “William passed away at home on 23rd July, 2026. We are deeply saddened by his passing. He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship, and kindness.” A cause of death has not been made public. Madonna paid tribute to Orbit on Instagram, writing: “He pressed a magic button inside of me and I fell into a galaxy of unrealized dreams. Your music gave me a magic carpet to fly on. You were my Ray of Light – as was my daughter Lola who was born around this time.” Among William Orbit’s many remix credits is his 1993 rework of Depeche Mode‘s “Walking in My Shoes”, released as the “Random Carpet Mix” and issued as part of the single’s release campaign for “Songs of Faith and Devotion”. About William Orbit William Orbit began his career in 1980 as a founding member of the ambient trio Torch Song, alongside Laurie Mayer and Grant Gilbert. He went on to score the 1986 film “Youngblood” and recorded as part of the dance act Bassomatic before establishing himself as a solo artist and in-demand remixer through the 1990s, working with artists including Madonna, U2, Kraftwerk, Nitzer Ebb and Blur. Orbit produced Madonna’s “Ray of Light” (1998), which won three Grammy Awards, and went on to work with her again on “Music” (2000) and “MDNA” (2012). He also produced Blur’s 1999 album “13” and delivered two UK number-one singles for All Saints, “Pure Shores” and “Black Coffee”. His solo output includes the long-running “Strange Cargo” series and the classical-crossover project “Pieces in a Modern Style”. His most recent solo album, “The Painter”, was released in 2022.

items.body: Finnish alt-electronic artist Detalji has released “So Call (Summer Night)”, a new single on the label Deep Limit, out August 12, 2026. The track is the latest cut from Detalji’s upcoming album “Imagine Life”, due October 16, 2026. “So Call (Summer Night)” was written about a specific memory. “This song was distilled directly from a certain memory,” Detalji said. “I remember partying at a midsummer festival with my friends, being intoxicated and happy at that moment listening to techno music and dancing the entire night. And at the same time being excited that I had met a certain special person, and that even though things were uncertain and they were far away, I was feeling hopeful and falling in love with the person and just feeling thankful for being alive. At that moment I felt the world was full of possibilities.” “Imagine Life” spans nine tracks: “Dancing (With What’s Left)”, “I Ain’t Faking”, “Circa 1983”, “Another Failed Romance”, “Bring Me Back to Life”, “Drifting”, “To The Night”, “Morning After” and “So Call (Summer Night)”. The album was written across Helsinki, Los Angeles and Berlin. Detalji describes it as centered on navigating contradiction and the pull between nostalgia and moving forward. “Imagine Life is a glimpse into a year of my life,” Detalji said. “I was moving between different cities, ending a relationship and figuring out what kind of life I wanted next. The album feels like a mixture of LA sunsets, Nordic melancholy and gritty Berlin basement beats.” About Detalji Detalji is an alt-electronic artist based in Finland who released the debut album “Truly” in 2023, featuring the single “Keep Me Alive”. Detalji has performed at SXSW, Eurosonic and Iceland Airwaves. “Imagine Life”, Detalji’s follow-up album, moves between electronica, trip-hop, house, drum & bass and synth textures, with “So Call (Summer Night)” marking one of its final singles ahead of the October 16 release.

items.body: Project Pitchfork, the Hamburg group that mixes dark wave, electro-industrial and dark electro elements, released “Quantum Mechanics” on 12 August 2011 through Trisol. The album turns 15 this year. It arrived one year after “Continuum Ride” (2010) and appeared on CD, as a strictly limited double-CD book edition of 2,000 copies, and digitally. Peter Spilles wrote and produced the album, Chris von Rautenkranz mastered it at Soundgarden Tonstudio, Ingo Römling created the artwork and Jens Howorka took the band photography. The ten-track album runs “Freeze in Silence,” “Lament,” “Run for Cover,” “Radical Business,” “Mute Spectators,” “Quantum Mechanics,” “The Queen of Time and Space,” “Splice,” “We Will Descend” and “You Rest in My Heart.” The book edition, bound with thread stitching and packed with a 40-page booklet of lyrics and additional artwork, adds a bonus disc holding the exclusive tracks “Tempest” and “Insomnia,” remixes of “Freeze in Silence,” “Run for Cover” and “Lament,” and an instrumental version of the title track. In December 2019, Trisol reissued “Quantum Mechanics” as a limited 2LP and 2CD set. The album streams on Spotify. About Project Pitchfork Project Pitchfork started in Hamburg, Germany, where vocalist and composer Peter Spilles and keyboardist Dirk Scheuber began collaborating in 1989. The pair played their first concert in Hamburg in February 1990 and recorded the demo “K.N.K.A.” that same year. Their debut album “Dhyani” followed in May 1991 on Hypnobeat, and 1992 brought both “Lam-‘Bras,” which introduced vocalist Patricia Nigiani, and “Entities.” In 1994 the band moved to Off Beat for “IO,” whose singles “Renascence” and “Carrion” brought them into the German charts. A year later they founded their own imprint Candyland Entertainment, issued “Alpha Omega” and supported Rammstein on selected tour dates. The late 1990s produced “¡Chakra:Red!” and the concept album “Eon:Eon,” while the 2000s added “Daimonion,” the “NUN” trilogy built around “Inferno,” and “Kaskade” (2005). On Trisol, the group released “Dream, Tiresias!” and “Continuum Ride” before “Quantum Mechanics” arrived in August 2011. “Black” (2013), “Blood” (2014) and “Look Up, I’m Down There” (2016) followed, and the space-oriented trilogy of “Akkretion,” “Fragment” and “Elysium” was completed in 2024. The current line-up centres on Peter Spilles with keyboardist Jürgen Jansen and drummers Achim Färber and Christian “Leo” Leonhardt; co-founder Dirk Scheuber left the group in 2021. The 15th anniversary of “Quantum Mechanics” places the album back in that timeline, early in the band’s 2010s run on Trisol.

items.body: German synth-pop duo Purwien & Kowa release the single “Hinter Glas” on August 14, 2026 via Town And Towers Records. The track is a new version of “Hinter Glas,” a song originally released by Christian Purwien’s earlier band Second Decay, and arrives ahead of the duo’s sixth studio album, “Sechs,” due October 9, 2026 on the same label. The digital single carries three tracks: “Hinter Glas,” a remix of “Eyes Of Aragon” by Swedish electronic duo CRED, and a 12″ mix of “Hinter Glas.” “Eyes Of Aragon” was originally recorded by No Comment, the German synth-pop band Thomas Kowa played in from 1989. The single is available on major streaming services through this link. Purwien & Kowa reunite Second Decay and No Comment on ‘Hinter Glas’ “Hinter Glas” first appeared on Second Decay‘s 1993 maxi-CD of the same name and again a year later on the album “Taste,” the German wave/electronic act Christian Purwien co-founded with Andreas Michael Sippel in 1987. With Purwien & Kowa, Purwien re-recorded his own song while Thomas Kowa brought in a remix of “Eyes Of Aragon” from his former band No Comment, handled by CRED. The pairing puts a track from each half of the duo’s back catalogue on a single release. Purwien & Kowa describe their own sound as “retro analogue synth pop without hair.” “Hinter Glas” follows the single “Concorde” as the second preview of “Sechs,” the duo’s sixth studio album, due October 9, 2026 via Town And Towers Records. The band also runs the Disko 80 podcast with Purwien and Kowa as hosts, and records as Heldautomat as a side project. About Purwien & Kowa Purwien & Kowa is a German synth-pop duo based in Dortmund formed by Christian Purwien and Thomas Kowa. Purwien co-founded the electronic/darkwave act Second Decay in 1987, initially under the name Blue Velvet, together with Andreas Michael Sippel. Second Decay released the tape “Monochromes” in 1988 and the 12-inch “Killing Desire” in 1989, followed by “La Décadence Électronique” on CD in 1992, the “Hinter Glas” maxi-CD in 1993 and the album “Taste” in 1994. The band continued with “Der Nerv” in 1995, “Familiar” in 1997, “The Hunt” and “De Luxe” in 1998, “Hotels” in 1999 and “Kaltes, weißes Licht” in 2001, before pausing new material after the 2002 live release “Zwischenfall 1999.” Thomas Kowa, born Thomas Kowalzik in 1969 in Ludwigshafen am Rhein, joined the German synth-pop band No Comment in 1989 and has lived in Switzerland since 2007. He founded the label Nanopop in 2001, closing it in 2007 to focus on writing; since 2012 he has published a series of crime novels and thrillers. His other current music projects include Nine Seconds and Emily Kinski’s dead. Purwien and Kowa began recording together as Purwien & Kowa, releasing the three-EP digital set “Drei” via Zwei Records in October 2018. The duo also co-hosts the Disko 80 podcast, which covers 1980s music and has featured more than 100 episodes with guests including Joachim Witt, Bernhard Lloyd of Alphaville and Marcus Meyn of Camouflage. Kowa separately co-hosts the “Krimi Schweiz” podcast on Swiss crime fiction. Purwien & Kowa returned in 2026 with the single “Concorde,” followed by “Hinter Glas,” ahead of their sixth studio album “Sechs,” due October 9, 2026 via Town And Towers Records.

Purwien began his recording career in 1987 as co-founder and vocalist of Second Decay, a project originally named Blue Velvet, alongside Andreas Sippel. Working exclusively with analogue synthesizers, Second Decay released the tape “Monochromes” in 1988, the 12-inch “Killing Desire” in 1989, the CD “La Décadence Électronique” in 1992, the maxi-CD “Hinter Glas” in 1993 and the album “Taste” in 1994, the release that introduced “Anders Sein.” Second Decay’s second album, “The Hunt,” originally released in 1996, was reissued by Emmobiz Records as a green double LP with bonus tracks in November 2025, and a second vinyl edition of “Taste” followed via Emmo.Biz Records in 2026. Heldautomat, launched in 2026 with the single “Am ersten Tag,” is described by the duo as a darker and more uncompromising direction than their earlier collaborative work, built around analogue synthesizers, piano and minimalist drum-machine rhythms. “Anders Sein” is the project’s second single, revisiting a track from Purwien’s own back catalogue ahead of the debut Heldautomat album “Zwischen den Lichtern,” due in autumn 2026.
